subsubtopic: ATTITUDE OF CANADA AT THE OUTBREAK OF HOSTILITIES, 1938-39
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to
table parliamentary return reference No. 33, moved by the hon. member for St. John-Albert:
For a copy of all correspondence, letters, cables and other documents exchanged between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and His Majesty's government in Canada from September 1, 1938, to September 15, 1939, relating to the attitude of Canada in the event of an outbreak of hostilities between His Majesty and any other power.
When the motion was adopted the order was extended to cover a period subsequent to September 15 sufficient to complete the correspondence in reference to the particular matters referred to.
I would say that the reason for the delay in bringing down this return is that the consent of the government of the United Kingdom and the consent of the government of Australia and New Zealand had to be obtained before we felt at liberty to table the correspondence. That consent has now been obtained, and the return which I have just made includes all the correspondence.
Previous to September 1, 1939, the government of Canada was kept informed of international developments in the usual manner. As the crisis approached in the summer of 1939 there were consultations between the United Kingdom and Canadian authorities through the United Kingdom high commissioner at Ottawa and the Canadian high commissioner in the United Kingdom.
I think hon. members will find this return most interesting and of historic interest, inasmuch as it relates to the attitude of Canada at the outbreak of hostilities between His Majesty and the German Reich. There are only eight telegrams in all; they are not very lengthy, and I believe it would meet the convenience of hon. members if they were printed in the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons. I ask that instructions be given accordingly.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO CANADIAN PRESS CORRESPONDENTS
subsubtopic: BOARDING TROOPSHIPS IN NEW YORK HARBOUR
speechtext: Yesterday in my absence the leader of the opposition asked, in view of the fact that press representatives were not allowed on the Queen Elizabeth at her recent visit at New York, whether steps would be taken to allow such representatives to board ships arriving in future in New York with returning Canadian service personnel. Perhaps I can best answer that by explaining what steps were taken to have them allowed on board this time. I was advised two or three days before the ship was due that the regulations at New York did not permit of press representatives being allowed on board. They had been, of course, when the ship called at Halifax. I asked the quartermaster-general to endeavour to get that ruling changed. He was not successful. We then took it up through our minister at Washington. He discussed it with the war department and with the department of state. The United States war department and state department said that they would waive their objections: they had no objection to the rule being changed so far as Canadian press men were concerned, although it might involve some difficulty with United States newspaper men wTho were not allowed on their transports. However, the owners of the ship, the Ounard-Whi'te Star -line, were not prepared to allow the regulation to be changed, and therefore it was not possible for Canadian newsmen to go on board.

BONUS OR SUBSIDY ON WOOD FUEL
speechtext:
1.	When was payment by the government of bonus or subsidy on wood fuel in Canada commenced?
2.	During what period was it paid?
3.	What department of government made such payments?
4.	At what rate was it paid?
5.	What was the total amount so paid to wood dealers in Yukon?

7.	What proceedings is an applicant required to take to obtain such payments as yet not made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BONUS OR SUBSIDY ON WOOD FUEL
speechtext:
1.	Subsidies authorized by P.C. 3465, April 29, 1943, and subsequent orders in council have been payable, subject to varying conditions on wood fuel delivered to a dealer or held for his account on and after March 5, 1943. (By P.C. 7802 dated Oct. 6, 1944 subsequent payments of subsidy were restricted to wood fuel delivered to or held for a dealer's accounts after Sept. 30, 1945.)
2.	Subsidies have been payable, subject to varying conditions, since the passage of P.C. 3465, April 29, 1943, and continue to be payable.

3.	Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Ltd. on the directions of the timber controller (originally the coal controller, followed by the wood fuel controller during the successive periods in which wood fuel was under their respective jurisdictions.)
4.	Subject to certain limitations, subsidy was payable at the rate of SI.00 per standard cord of 128 cubic feet on wood fuel contracted for and cut on or before Dec. 31, 1944, and delivered to a dealer or held for his account on and after March 5, 1943. (By P.C. 7802 dated Oct. 6, 1944 subsequent payments of subsidy were restricted to wood fuel delivered to or held for a dealer's accounts after Sept. 30, 1945.)
Subject to certain limitations, subsidy was payable on wood fuel as described above covering such portion of the wood fuel dealers' transportation costs as the timber controller might specify.
Subject to certain limitations, subsidy is payable to wood fuel dealers on the certification of the timber controller on such transactions and in such localities where, in the judgment of the timber controller, a subsidy or bonus is necessary, having regard to the costs of production and transportation, to get the

Questions
necessary quantity of wood fuel produced and transported. The rate at which such subsidy is payable is specified by the timber controller in each individual case.
5.	To Sept. 30, 1945, subsidy amounting to $2,158.45 has been paid to wood fuel dealers in the Yukon.
6.	No final date for the discontinuance of subsidies on wood fuel has yet been established.
7.	To obtain a subsidy a dealer must apply to the regional wood fuel officer, Vancouver (British Columbia and Yukon) for an eligibility, giving full particulars of his anticipated costs of purchase and of handling the particular lot of wood in question. If, in the opinion of the regional wood fuel officer, such wood is really required and a subsidy is necessary, the eligibility will be granted. Then when the dealer has bought and moved that wood to his yard or delivered it to his customers, he must apply for the agreed subsidy stating the exact costs incurred and attaching to his application evidence in the shape of receipts that such expenditures were actually made. The necessary forms are supplied by the regional wood fuel officer.
Subsidies, varying according to the needs in each particular instance, are payable to licensed wood fuel dealers:
(a)	in the discretion of the timber controller ;
(b)	where there are definite shortages of wood fuel in consuming centres;

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution.
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act to provide for payment of an allowance to every member of the Senate and House of Commons for expenses incidental to his duties as a member at the rate of two thousand dollars per annum for the period during which he is a member, payable at the end of each calendar year and subject to a deduction equal to one-half of the amount of deductions, if any, from the member's allowances in respect of sittings of the house of which he is a member during such year, and to provide that in the case of ministers of the crown, of the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, and of members of the Senate the amount of such allowance shall be deemed to be taxable income; and to provide further that such measure shall be deemed to have come into effect on the sixth day of September, one thousand nine hundred and forty-five.
He said: As my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), in leading the house last night, announced at the close of the session, in bringing forward this particular motion I desire to substitute it for one which is already on the order paper as order No. 7. Hon. members will notice that order No. 7 relates only to members of the House of Commons. The resolution now .presented is in more complete form and has reference to members of the Senate as well as members of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Senate and House of Commons
May I say a word with respect to the circumstance that the resolution should have appeared on the order paper in the first instance with reference only to members of the House of Commons.
When the resolution was placed on the order paper in the form in which it was it represented the only decision which had been arrived at by the government up to that time with respect to allowances to members of parliament for expenses incidental to their duties as members of parliament.
It was obviously desirable that there should be discussion with members of the senate before deciding on what should appear in resolution form with respect to members of that house. I did not have any opportunity to have a discussion with members of the upper house before leaving for England, and subsequently visiting the United States. When my colleagues in the government saw that I would be returning sooner than was expected at the time I left, it was decided by them to leave over discussion w'ith representatives of the senate until after my return. When I returned I found a great many matters demanding urgent attention, and it was not possible for me to arrange to see representative members of the senate immediately. I took the first chance I had to discuss with some of the senators the position of members in the other house in respect to the expenses incidental to the discharge of their duties, and I have since gone more fully into the matter with representative members of that house. The measure which I now bring before the house is one which in its more complete form will, I think, commend itself to members of both houses of parliament-at any rate, I sincerely hope that that may be so.
At this late stage of the session, Mr. Speaker, I may have to ask the house for its unanimous consent to allow me to proceed a little more rapidly with consideration of the motion now before us than might otherwise be the case. When the orders of the day are reached I shall ask that the house allow the motion No. 7, which is now in its possession, to be withdrawn and the order to be discharged. I make that intention known immediately so that we may be in a position to discuss the resolution that now appears under government notices of motion.
With respect to this notice of motion I would say that His Excellency the Governor General, having been informed of the subject matter of this resolution, is pleased to recommend it to the consideration of the house.
With the permission of the house, I would now ask that the necessary steps be taken

to proceed at once in committee with the resolution in order that I may have an opportunity of introducing the bill immediately. I should think that all the discussion that may be necessary can be had on the second reading of the bill. If the house will give its unanimous consent to this procedure, I shall see that the bill is introduced this morning with the understanding that discussion upon it will not take place before tomorrow.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
subsubtopic: ALLOWANCE OF $2,000 TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT FOR INCIDENTAL EXPENSES
speechtext: I rise just for a moment to say that I am opposed to this measure. I cannot conceive of anything more unwise for this parliament to do at a time when the affairs of the country are in such a state as they are, and when this house has failed to take any action which would relieve the present distress of the great mass of the people of the country, than to pass this resolution. The distress is increasing daily, and we have done nothing in the house to alleviate it. We have failed to deal with old age pensions and with increasing unemployment. Veterans in my own city of Vancouver are unemployed by the thousands. I consider therefore that this action by this House of Commons is a colossal impudence.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext: In view of what has just been said I too feel that I must say something, although I did not intend to do so. I fully -appreciate the remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East. All of us in this group at least, and I think throughout the house, feel exactly the same way about the condition of the people generally in the country, and if I thought that the defeat of this resolution would bring relief to these people I would support the opposition to it. But obviously their condition will no-t be helped by members of parliament -remaining in the position in which they have found themselves over a period of years. Some members of parliament I know are moving into further debt and having their work made ineffective by the care that has been put upon -them in that respect. In the -early days of our parliamentary history the House of Commons was looked upon as a place where gentlemen met; as the best club in London, and perhaps-I do not know about Canada-as the best club in Ottawa. Fortunately for democracy that day has gone, and there are members in this House of Commons now who -of necessity must give all their time to the business of the country, meet unusual expenses, and who are expected to get by on an amount which in the past has been altogether inadequate. That, I think, is particularly true of some of us in this group.

speechtext:
I respect the view's of my colleague. Some may differ with us; they are not many, but it is their view and they have a right to it. But they are wrong, because the indemnity received by members goes back to their constituents; it goes to hotels and transportation companies for trips for which we pay from our own pockets, though they are for the benefit of our constituents. A member who does not touch the pork barrel cannot possibly live on an indemnity which by taxation has been reduced to $2,800. It is not now a question of ethics. The real question is obvious: shall it be possible for poor men to remain inpolitics, or shall politics become on-ly the realm of the rich? The -hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the C.C.F. party, spoke very well, but perhaps he did not catch my remark when I said that in olden times members of parliament were elected by rotten boroughs. That was before the reform bill. At that time they were elected by a handful of people, and the common people had not the right to say who should be their member. That member apparently was

Senate and House oj Commons
the tool of a marquis or a duke or the owner of a large property, and the common man was ignored until the reform bill came along. But surprisingly enough in that land of contrasts, those were the top days of parliament. Precisely when members of parliament were elected by rotten boroughs, parliament reached its peak in England.
Well, this does not reflect Canadian conditions of to-day. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that some hon. members have been incurring debts while in politics. It is a fine gesture to say we will not touch it or that it should not be exempt from income tax. I remember the first lady who was elected to this house. In a very indignant mood, the first time she received $4,000 she went to her bank and obtained a certified cheque for $2,000 to the order of the Receiver General of Canada and said, "We are paid too much; S2,000 is enough. I will return $2,000 to the exchequer." She did that only once. At the time it was a fine gesture, giving money back to the exchequer. Why should we do that when we have to borrow more money from the bank? Let us be sensible, sir. The constituents of every member of this committee of the whole know very well what a member has to pay for: all sorts of celebrations; bazaars; wreaths; wedding gifts, and so on. They expect it; they think each member of parliament is a press making money.

I remember that once when I was sitting in the other corner there and we were discussing certain matters affecting ourselves, I spoke of members who were poor. Some gentlemen who are now in the senate, and who are very dear friends of mine, did not object to that; it was true. But another hon. gentleman who was my deskmate did object. He thought we should not say anything like that, that we should keep up appearances and never admit we were poor. Why pose as wealthy when we are not? And if we are not, it is precisely because we have done our duty. We have not touched the pork barrel; we have gone into debt just to serve our constituents.

The indemnity is not a salary; it is just a compensation for what we lose by sitting here for such long periods of time. I will not labour the question, Mr. Chairman, though there is much more I could say. Let us be sensible; let us be honest with the people. I am sure no hon. member will receive letters of protest, except from perhaps one or two of his constituents who are not familiar with the conditions that exist to-day.

speechtext:
I had not intended to speak on the resolution but since others have made some comments perhaps I should say a word as to the obligation I have felt in the matter of introducing this resolution. I speak now more particularly to hon. members who have come into the house since the last session, the last parliament in fact. Hon. members who were present at that time will remember that before the end of the session I stated that I thought the allowance paid to members of parliament was wholly inadequate, having regard to their increased obligations, the changed situation in the world, and the corresponding enlargement of their duties since the allowance had been previously fixed.
It was twenty-five years ago that parliament sanctioned its last increase in allowances to members of parliament. In the last session of the last parliament I said I should like to see an increase made at once, before the close of the session. I gave as a reason something which I since have had reason to believe was sound indeed. I pointed out that it was necessary to have in parliament, in these days, men of wide experience, men of known character and ability, men who were prepared to give a considerable portion of their time to the study of questions, as well as to speaking upon them. I pointed out further that, with the obligations of the members being what they are, it was becoming increasingly difficult to get the desirable type of persons to stand as candidates for the different parties. When I say this I am not referring to any one party, but to all parties.
I said at that time that I did not know what the fortunes of the political parties might be in the general election. I was not at all sure at that session that I would be standing where I am at the present time. I was not sure at that time that to-day I would even be where

Senate and House of Commons
my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) now sits. But I said that, in parliament or out of parliament, I would publicly advocate an increase in the allowances to be paid to members of parliament, and that this would be done for the sake of parliament itself and for the independence of individual members of parliament. I am now fulfilling that undertaking. May I add that the undertaking was made before the general election, and that during the campaign I repeated what I had said. I did so because I have a very high opinion of the institution of parliament. It is the most important of all the institutions in our country; no other is comparable with it. Those who come to parliament as members have not oply the obligations of legislators, but also of trustees of the financial and other resources of the country.
When the allowance was last increased the total appropriations of parliament were $568,939,431. In the last three sessions the appropriations were not in millions but in billions and were as follows: In 1942-43, $4,343,738,428; 1943-44, $5,540,668,592, and in 1944-45, $5,179483,114. In addition to that, at the time the allowance to members was last decided upon, in 1919-20, discussions in parliament related almost completely to matters of domestic concern. They dealt only to a limited extent with international affairs. That condition is not comparable at all with what we have to-day. In these days the whole of the discussions in parliament are on a very much vaster scale than anything known hitherto. And they are not going to become less. I venture to say that every question of real importance to-day has an international bearing and cannot be considered apart from its international bearing. I go further and say that our discussions already have demonstrated that we are dealing in large part with world problems. Every member in the house has been considering or discussing questions relating not to Canada alone, but to the world situation; and we are not going to go back, so far as discussions of the kind are concerned. New problems will become increasingly difficult and complex, and wall require more in the way of careful study and application of conscience on the part of all who are entrusted by the country with the discharge of public affairs.

Yes; my hon. friend has referred to time. I had occasion to look into the amount of time hon. members sat when the indemnity was last increased. I find that in 1920 the house sat 86 days, as compared with the session 1940-42, when it sat 105 days; that of 1942-43, when it sat 124 47696-215
days; 1943-44, 120 days, and 1944-45, 135 days. It will be noted that these are much longer periods of time than were customary when the last change was made.
Sometimes one hears comparisons made between the amounts received by members of parliament and salaries received by men in industry, wages paid, and the like. We heard a suggestion, very well intentioned, of one such comparison this morning. If I were to go back to my college days in search of an appropriate expression to meet any comparison I believe I would say that a member of parliament is in a position sui generis, that is to say, is in a position of his own; is in a class by himself. From the point of view of responsibility and opportunity combined, there is, or should be, no position held by any person in the country that can be compared with that of a member of parliament, whether he or she be in the House of Commons or in the Senate. I say that we belittle this greatest of all institutions for the preservation of liberty if in any way we seek to detract from the importance of parliament or if we do not afford to members of parliament that which will help to preserve their independence, or cause the best men in the country to enter its halls.
There are only a few members of the house who have not some business of their own, some professional or business obligations. These interests, to a considerable extent, to say nothing of family obligations, they must sacrifice while attending to the business of parliament. In these callings and professions they meet with difficulties which have to be met as if they were not serving as well the interests of the country as a whole.
I repeat, I believe the institution of parliament is the great palladium of liberty; it is the one institution above all others which can preserve freedom, it is more needed to-day than it has ever been in the world's history. A member of parliament, whether a member of the House of Commons or of the Senate, carries a burden upon his soul the like of which has never been placed upon the souls of men at any time heretofore, because it involves, as must now be clear to all hon. members, the question whether in the future we are to have life or death for mankind.
Mr. Speaker, I leave the matter there.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence? It was reported in the press yesterday that after December 15, the Lady Nelson would be used for transporting to this country the wives and other dependents of soldiers. Has the minister a statement to make on that matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT TO ASSUME FUNCTIONS OF RECONSTRUCTION AND MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend told me that he was going to ask this question, and I am glad that he has done so because the session will be over in a day or two and it might be well for me to state just what the position now is.
The basic policy governing the repatriation of soldiers and war brides from the United Kingdom remains unchanged. Very briefly this policy, as hon. members are already aware, is that no major movement of dependents will be undertaken until all troops who are available for repatriation, and have priority rights, have been returned to Canada. However, recent developments have now placed us in a more favourable position than was previously anticipated.
By the end of this month we shall have repatriated since V-E day slightly more than
180,000	soldiers in addition to Royal Canadian Navy and Royal Canadian Air Force personnel, leaving approximately 100,000 soldiers to return from overseas. This latter figure includes the occupation force of 25,000 and repatriation and other controlling staffs in the United Kingdom. This position is sufficiently favourable to justify our planning to allot in the latter part of January, and thereafter, an increased amount of shipping to repatriation of dependents without prejudice to the early repatriation of servicemen still abroad. The ships we propose employing for the return of dependents are our two hospital ships, the Lady Nelson and the Letitia. The Lady Nelson arrives in Canada on December 15 on its last trip with battle casualties. There will be, of course, a small

Income War Tax
number of casualties to service personnel resulting from accidents and- sickness, and these will continue to be returned to Canada by hospital ship; the remaining space will be made available to dependents. It is estimated that the Lady Nelson is capable of carrying between 200 and 300 dependents and can make about three round trips every two months.
The Letitia is at present in Vancouver where she is undergoing normal maintenance. She will return to England, via the Panama canal, and be dry-docked for necessary repairs and it is anticipated will be available for transatlantic runs about the end of January. We plan on employing this hospital ship in the same manner as the Lady Nelson. The Letitia can accommodate approximately 400 dependents, and can also do about three round trips in two months.
At the moment a strong possibility exists that in addition to these two ships at an early day we will be able to divert the Lady Rodney to carrying dependents. This ship was recently taken off the Newfoundland run and is now employed on troop carrying. The Lady Rodney has a capacity for approximately 250 to 300 dependents.
I wish to point out here that the carrying of dependents presents different problems from those incurred in the carrying of troops, and only certain ships are suitable for repatriating war brides with any economy of carrying capacity. Ships which carry dependents must have additional stewardesses and other ship staffs. They must be stocked with crockery and have suitable dining facilities; and in addition have different sanitary arrangements from those provided on our troopships.
The government is, and always has been, fully aware of the desirability of returning to Canada the dependents of Canadian soldiers at the earliest possible moment consistent with the rights of service personnel having repatriation priority. It therefore affords me no little pleasure to be able to inform the house of this shipping which is being made available at an earlier day than had hitherto been considered possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement to the house regarding this proposed amendment relating to the taxation of annuities. The committee may recall that when we were discussing the resolution on which the amendment is based I stated that the question of defining the capital element to be excluded from annuity payments for tax purposes was a very complicated one. The amendment I am now proposing to the bill which is before the committee is simpler and, at the same time, more generous to the taxpayer than the existing provision in the bill.
The amendment which I 'am now submitting provides that the capital element to be
Income War Tax

excluded from annuity payments Shall be based on either the commuted value of the annuity at the time it begins or the amount which the annuitant could, under the contract, have chosen to receive in lieu of the annuity if this amount is stated in the contract.
I should like to point out that the main problem that has had to be faced in connection with annuities is the possibility in certain cases of tax avoidance if the commuted value or optional lump sum payment is used, as is proposed in this amendment, as the basis for excluding the capital element in annuities. The possibility of abuse is in connection with deferred annuities where a large lump sum payment is made for an annuity to begin many years in the future, and the annuity may be an annuity certain for a very few years. Under such an arrangement a person would, in effect, secure tax exemption on the interest earnings of this large amount of capital which would have accumulated over the period of deferment. Possibly I have in my own mind exaggerated the importance of this danger, but I did not feel justified in presenting to the house legislation which would be subject to criticism along the lines I have just suggested. I think, however, that the proviso at the end of the amendment I have just moved will be a sufficient safeguard against the tax avoidance possibilities in the device I have just mentioned. The proviso states that notwithstanding this provision (meaning the provision relating to the exclusion of the capital element from annuity payments) the minister may, in any case in which he considers it proper to do so, exercise the powers conferred on him by subsection 2 of this section.
Subsection 2 just referred to states as follows:
"Where, under any existing or future contract or arrangement for the payment of money, the minister is of the opinion
(a)	that payments of principal money and interest are blended, or
(b)	payment is made pursuant to a plan which involves an allowance of interest,
Whether or not there is any provision for payment of interest at a nominal rate or at all, the minister shall have the power to determine what part of any such payment is interest, and the part so determined to be interest shall be deemed to be income for the purposes of this act."
This section, gives the minister power to deal effectively with any tax evasion which might be prompted through the somewhat generous provision with respect to the taxation of the interest element in annuities.
I had better read the amendment and send copies to those who are interested in the bill. The amendment is:
That the following be substituted for paragraph (b) in lines 9 to 30, page 1:
(b) annuities received under a contract (other than payments described in paragraph
(c)	of this subsection) except a portion of each amount received thereunder that bears the same relation to the whole amount as the amount that the annuitant could, under the the contract, have chosen to receive in lieu of the annuity or, if no such choice is provided by the contract, the present value (computed in such manner as the minister may by regulation prescribe) of the annuity at the time of commencement thereof, bears to the aggregate computed in the case of an annuity for life on the assumption that the annuitant will live during the period of his normal expectation of life (calculated in accordance with mortality tables approved by the minister) of the *annuity for which the contract provides:
Provided that this provision shall not be construed to prejudice the operation of subsection 2 of this section.

I wish to raise a question in regard to subparagraph (g) at the top of page 2, which reads:
All annuities and other annual payments received under the provisions of a will or trust ...
What I wish to draw particular attention to is line ten:
... except a payment or portion thereof which can be established by the recipient not to have been paid out of the income of the estate or trust.
I am questioning the words "can be established", because I think they may go a very long way, and I have an alternative to suggest. Perhaps it is familiar to the minister, but I want to make this comment, which I think is a valid one. This is in aid not of the big man, but of the small man, because the small annuitant can never go to the expense of trying to have the question determined, since the amount involved is not large enough. I will read the alternative so that the minister can decide whether it is satisfactory. It seems to me to be proper, and I press strongly the significance of those words "which can be established by the recipient". They put all the onus on the recipient, and that involves a great deal of difficulty. The alternative I have to suggest is this:
except that portion of the annuity payment or other annual payments received under _ the provisions of any will or trust which is derived from the income of the estate or trust irrespective of the date on which the will or trust became effective, whether the same is received in periods longer than or shorter than one year.
In other words, the only change is to remove the onus from the recipient. That onus can be a very heavy one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The onus was put on the recipient to cover a case something like this. Suppose there is an estate, the income from which is $10,000. The testator does not know exactly what the income of his estate is going to be, but probably he assumes that the income will be more than that. He leaves eleven annuities of $1,000 each. Now each annuitant will claim that his $1,000 came, not out of the $10,000 but out of capital. They will all claim that their annuities came out of capital. There is $1,000 there that has to be accounted for.
Somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. There are eleven annuities, and, as I say, each will claim that his annuity comes out of capital. That has to be settled among themselves or by the executor or someone else. It cannot be left to the minister, because it will mean that the minister would have power to decide the question. If you gave the minister discretion he would apportion it, and say that a small portion came out of capital with reference to each annuity. It has to be left to the people themselves, the trustee or the executor of the estate to say where that extra $1,000 came
Income War Tax

from, whether from capital or income. It must be settled by them. The minister cannot run around trying to prove that it came out of income rather than out of capital. It was to cover a case such as that that the burden was put on the recipient, and it is not a heavy burden.

In the first place, I think the minister will agree that the case he mentions is not a usual one. In fact it is fairly remote. In the second place, after all, the wording I suggest simply means that the people themselves will have to establish what the truth is. They cannot simply make a statement without evidence. "That portion of the annuity payment or other annual payments received under the provisions of any will or trust which is derived from the income of the estate or trust" is a matter of fact. I am satisfied that the minister, as a lawyer, or a reformed lawyer, will agree with me that when you put that onus on the recipient it can create a very substantial additional burden. It is not a. case of hair-splitting. I submit that what it does do is to put a substantial additional burden on those who already have a heavy burden to carry. They would just come along and say that it is from the income without giving any reason to substantiate it. They are taxed with this heavy onus which can be established by the recipient.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

31.000	a year, but if he says nothing and does not need to say anything, who in the world can say which annuitant drew the money out of capital? This makes him say, and he must say. In the absence of this he does not need to say anything at all; he just pays out the
311.000	a year and he leaves it to the minister. The minister starts to tax somebody because it came out of income, and each one he starts to tax says, "No, mine came out of capital." The minister says, "Why do you say it came out of capital?" The man says, "I do not need to say anything about it; you have to show it came out of income." You cannot show it came out of income because there was not enough income. That is the position we are trying to avoid. It is not a great burden for any of those people. All they need to do is to show that they got the annuities out of income. Where the annuities are greater than the income I suppose they will arrange it so

that the person with the largest income got the annuities out of capital, because they save more taxes that way.

This is a case that will arise often. Either it should be made definite here or it should be left to the minister, because the executor has no power to deal with it. The only occasion I know of on which power like that is given to an executor is where a trust company have power under a will to allocate certain amounts paid for repairs between the life tenant and the reversioners, but they have no power to do anything except pay out money in the case of an annuity. This question will arise in the first instance in every case when the executor files the form which is prepared a month before the other forms are filed. He will say that so much income came from the estate, and on the back he has to show where it is allocated. He has to say that so much went to John Jones and so much to William Smith, and so forth. After he does that he lists the total amount of the income, and if he shows less than the total amount of the income the department immediately gets after them and makes somebody else pay the difference. He will have to do it in some way or other, or simply make a statement as to how it is paid. I submit that the executor must be helped by appropriate legislation. In the case of a deficiency it will be allocated against the different people who are interested in it, because you cannot get them all together to agree to it. Some of them may be in California, some in Vancouver, some in Toronto. They will not agree to it. The executors have no power. I believe this either can be covered by legislation or can be left to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think they will agree to it. If they do not agree, they will have to pay taxes on the whole thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not an easy way out of it to give the minister power to allocate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member's colleagues are willing.
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is giving another discretion to the minister.

The people who are handling estates have enough trouble without throwing this additional burden on the executors. It could be covered by an appropriate clause or by leaving it to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We believe this is the best way to get at it. It avoids giving the minister another discretion, and it really puts some responsibility on the beneficiaries in these rare cases. There will not be very many of them. They will come to some agreement, because if it is not established the whole thing is, taxable.

I really think the minister should meet these objections. Thousands of such cases are coming up every day. Surely we can assist the executors and everybody else. In the long run it would be assisting the minister. Why not put. in a clause covering that? We have never found the taxing officers anything but fair; at least I have not. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; it is an invidious sort of power to invest in the minister, to ask him to choose certain persons or to say that the annuity' comes out of income and they are fully taxable. We should not be asked to say to one individual that his comes out of income and to another that his does not. The burden to establish that should be on the people who are seeking tax relief. At the present time these annuities are fully taxable. They are being relieved of taxation to the extent that they come out of capital. Year after year we have had representations, if not in this House of Commons, outside of it, that it is wrong to tax annuities if they come out of capital. We have said: In those numerous cases how can we tell whether they come out of capital or not? That was just the trouble. In these cases we can let them find out and establish that it came out of capital, and then it is not taxed. I think it is perfectly fair.

I hesitate to raise this question again, but this is my first opportunity to do it. I refer to certain government annuities which, under this section, will be subjected to tax to which I believe they should not be subjected. Annuities were sold by the Department of Labour and its representatives to Canadian citizens. The number who purchased them, according ito the Ives commission report, totalled something over 100,000. ' Of that number those who are interested in the particular aspect of the case to -which I wish to draw attention probably number some 40,000 of our citizens, who with their families undoubtedly number over
100,000	Canadian people.
These government annuities were sold prior to June 25, 1940. In some cases they may have been paid for in full up to the maximum amount of SI ,200. In other cases the agents for the Department of Labour said: You may take out whatever amount is convenient for you now. The amounts stipulated ran from $100 to S600, as the case may be. They were told that they had the right at any time to enlarge the contract up to SI.200, and that the annuity would be tax free. When I said the other evening that the representatives of the Department of Labour made such statements the minister challenged my words. I find that there can be no contradiction of my remarks because these agents of the Department of Labour did go about the country and sold 100,000 or more annuities on that assumption. In proof of that statement I shall point to a booklet which was put out prior to June 25, 1940, called "An Old Age of Comfort and Happiness." On page 12 of this booklet, printed by the king's printer, I find the following:
The advantages of Canadian government annuities. A Canadian government annuity is the safest investment you can make. The security of the whole dominion is behind your purchase. It is free from dominion government taxation. . It is payable for life.
And so forth. This is the printed evidence on which these annuities were sold. What evidence is there that one has the right to enlarge the annuity? If one looks at the contract, for instance, he finds that there are certain conditions printed on it. It says:
If desired this contract (may be matured .at an earlier date than specified therein on any anniversary of the date of issue, the amount of annuity being adjusted accordingly, provided that the minimum annuity of $10 a year has been purchased.
I may say that that bears relation not so much to enlarging the annuity to $1,200 as to maturing it at an earlier date than originally suggested in the contract. However, there can be no doubt that the applicant for the annuity was given the right to enlarge that annuity under the same terms and conditions as those to which he originally subscribed. I will read again from an application form on which I see the wording in ink "June 16, 1936," and the address of the agent of the Canadian government annuities branch. It says:
... and with the understanding that such an annuity will in any event be granted to me as the" total amount paid in by me improved at four per cent compounded yearly will purchase at the rates in effect at the date of this application, the same not to exceed $1,200.
I mention that as tying the government down to the rates, and again I refer to the government publication, printed by the king's
Income War Tax

printer, in which these annuities are stated to be free from dominion government taxation. In 1940, however, the matter undoubtedly came to the attention of the income tax department. I think it may have come to its attention before that, because I believe one agent in Winnipeg sold some of these contracts on representations which were not desirable and had a great many people subscribe to them with nominal payments, though the practice probably was not as general as the minister may have believed. So in 1940, when the income tax rates became very high and it might have been possible for certain people who held these contracts for small amounts to enlarge them and thereby obtain a substantial advantage, much greater than they had ever contemplated prior to the war because no one foresaw that within a few short years the income tax rates of this country would be about equal to those in Great Britain, section 5(k) was passed by this house. At the time I drew the attention of the minister to this matter, and I thought I had made a blunt statement, though I did not speak with any fervour at all, when I said the minister had broken the word of the Dominion of Canada. At that time I understood him to agree, as Hansard for that day records; I quoted the sentence the other evening. The minister now claims he did not understand it, and even challenges my suggestion that the agents of the Department of Labour had made these representations in regard to annuities being tax free, which undoubtedly was the case. Section 5(k) went on to say:
... provided that such exemption shall not extend to that portion of the income which exceeds the amount of the annuity actually specified in the contract -before the 25th day of June, 1940 ...
That is to say, if you had subscribed for a $600 annuity, you could not enlarge it to $1,200. Then quoting again from the act:
... where such excess -amount -arises by reason of any option or contractual right to enlarge the annuity income by -the paymen-t of additional sums or premiums, unless such additional sums or premiums have actually been paid before the said date;
In order to break the warranty or the contract of the government with the citizens of the country it was necessary that this house actually say, in the budget brought down at that time by the minister, that notwithstanding any option or contractual right we would do so and so. Well, surely if you have a contract to purchase 160 -acres for a farm, and have an option to purchase the adjoining 160 acres, the option is as much a part of the contract as is the original purchase; there is [Mr. Jackman.1
no question about that. However, I did not want to make very much of the point at the time. In the first place the country needed the revenue, and in the second place I had no doubt at that time where the equity lay. I thought it lay primarily with the government, because people had taken out annuities for small amounts, -and with the great increase in income tax rates there was a tremendous unexpected advantage to the annuity holder. Nevertheless I say as solemnly as I can that it is my belief that the Minister of Finance, or whoever was responsible for it, did break the -word of the dominion government in that regard to a great many of our people.
That is the first matter I wish to speak about, having to do with the enlargement of these annuities taken out prior to 1940, which right was taken away -and the contract and word of the government broken in 1940. Now, however, I come to a matter which to me has much greater contractual significance, and where the equity lies not with the government but surely with the annuity holder. There were many, I estimate around forty thousand, annuity holders who took out these contracts, let us say, for the maximum of $1,200 prior to 1940, to mature perhaps twenty or thirty years later. Now, or some time in the near future, they wish to mature those contracts by paying in a sufficient amount of capital to enable them to draw their $1,200, which according to the terms -of the contract were to be at the same rates, and according to the representations made and well understood by everyone, to some extent so well understood that they are protected as to the amount paid in by the government in its legislation; that is, they were sold on the understanding that the income was to be free from dominion government taxation.
Well, after that legislation came down in 1940 some people had doubts as to whether they would be entirely free of tax in connection with these annuities taken out prior to 1940, even though they had stipulated for $1,200. Letters were written to the annuities branch of the Department of Labour asking whether or not these contracts had been prejudicially affected. The replies came back that the contracts which stipulated for $1,200, taken out prior to 1940, were in no way prejudicially affected. Letters to that effect will be found in the files of the annuities branch; and, if I am correctly informed, at that time an opinion was given by the Department of National Revenue that such annuities which stipulated for the maximum of $1,200 would not be taxed if they were made immediate. Section 5 (k) speaks of "enlargement" and

the question apparently was whether or not making an annuity immediate, the maturing of it, was an enlargement. From what I can understand, the first opinion given was that it was not an enlargement, and that any person holding a $1,200 annuity could pay it up in full. Then apparently there was a change of heart, probably because income tax rates were becoming steeper and apparently necessity knows no law, even when the dominion government is concerned in the case. Bo we find that the annuities branch issued a ruling in regard to income tax concerning these annuities, under date of July 10, 1944, in which they said:
However, exemption from income tax, shall not extend to that portion of the income which exceeds the amount of annuity-
I emphasize the word "amount" because it is the point at issue.
-actually specified in the contract-
There is only one amount specified in the
contract, and that is $1,200.
-before the 25th of June, 1940, where such excess amount of annuity arises by reason of any option or contractual right to enlarge the annuity income by the payment of additional sums or premiums unless such additional sums or premiums have actually been paid before the said date.
That ruling referred to the amount actually specified in the contract. That surely can mean only one thing; that is, as set out on the face of the contract. This announcement by the superintendent of annuities on July 10, 1944, was followed by one from the same branch of government on September 1, 1944, which was changed in wording and which did not make the same reference to the amount stipulated on the face of the contract.
Correspondence has also been had as to the contract, and such statements as these were made:
The contract may be converted into an immediate annuity to begin at an earlier anniversary date of the contract. Deposits may be made irregularly, and if a sufficient amount is deposited the date of maturity of the contract would be automatically brought forward.
In respect to the whole matter the holder of the annuity gained only one impression, and that was that contracts prior to 1940 were tax tree as to the stipulated amount, and that they could be matured at an earlier date if so desired.	[DOT]
I do not wish to say much more on the matter. The minister did not seem to be too familiar with all the details in connection with annuities when he spoke the other evening. A document which he recommended is, I find, a most interesting one-and I hope he has read it himself. I would refer to the first 47696-216
page of part I of the royal commission on the taxation of annuities and family corporations, 1945. It states:
The complaints and criticism of a considerable number who had purchased government annuity contracts prior to 25th June, 1940, when the present section 5 (k) of the act came into force, and who had contractual rights *therein to increase their annuities as their savings permitted, were strong and severe. They contend that they had no knowledge of the proposed change in time to protect themselves, but a much greater number complained that they purchased their annuities from the crown on the assurance of the department and its salesmen, and upon the statements in literature distributed by the government that the annuities they were invited to purchase would be exempt from all federal taxation.
For all time?

Until the annuities expired. They were sold on a distinct basis, and people who bought these bought them instead of other investments. That is why I say the dominion government has broken its bond, that it has broken the word of the Dominion of Canada in this regard. I do not believe there can be any contention to the contrary.
Since I made certain statements the last occasion the matter was before the committee, friends of mine and those with whom I have been associated, who have the utmost confidence in the word and integrity of the Minister of Finance-and perhaps also in my word -cannot believe that both the minister and I can be right in this matter. The responsible minister states on the one hand that the dominion government has not broken its word, while I contend that it has. And yet we find in the report of this royal commission the very proposition I am now putting before the committee.
Let me read the final sentence in the report of the royal commission, which I believe is as strong as any words I could use. That final sentence is this: "They feel that they have been betrayed by their government."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the commission does not say so.

I am reading from the summary of the evidence, and I should like to correct any wrong impression I might have created. This is the summary of evidence compiled by the commissioners, the evidence upon which the commission has reported. These are the complaints and criticisms of the holders of the annuities.
Did the commission say that?

They have not said anything about it, because it was not within the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I deny, as I did before, that the government has broken its word in this matter. I deny that there has been any betrayal. I can understand that there were certain purchasers of options- because that is really what they were-to increase annuities if they wished. The government was bound, but they were not bound to increase. I can understand that. These purchasers of options, when they found that this would be a very desirable form of investment into which they could put their money, felt that they would take up these options and put their moneys into annuities which would be totally free of taxation. Then they found that there had been a change in the law, so that they could not do that. But surely we carry out our contract with them when we permit them to enlarge their annuities. That was our contract.
It is not the same annuity at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our contract with them was to sell them an enlarged annuity. The contract had nothing in it about taxation. But surely if a person who is not bound at all, but who merely has an option to put his money into an enlarged annuity, chooses later to enlarge his annuity, he must take that enlarged annuity subject to the taxation prevailing at the time he enlarges it.

Whether they were fully paid annuities, or annuities with contractual rights, makes no difference. Surely it makes no difference whether a contract is a contract for a sale of goods, or a contract expressing an option or a right in the future. Both are valid in law. There is no question as to whether one has value and the other has not value. The option has just as much value as any contract in business. Will the minister say that these contracts, or options-call them what you like-were not sold by representatives of the government with the clear understanding that they, and their enlargements, if you wish, would be free from dominion government taxation? Does the minister deny that this is a booklet issued by the dominion government? I point out that it bears the king's printer's imprimatur. They were sold under warranty; there is no question about that.
The hon. member for Rosedale has laboured this point for some time. He did so when the resolutions were before us, and has done it again to-day.
And I will labour it again.

If the hon. member were minister and if he were introducing the legislation he is now advocating, would that be his plan? Even though there were salesmen who gave certain undertakings with those who entered into this contract, certainly the government did not assure those persons who made purchases that there never would be any change in the income tax laws. I think the hon. member for Rosedale was right when, during the war, he did not press his point.

I believe the principle at stake to be a very important one, first- because there are so many of our citizens who hold these annuity contracts, something over 100,000, I believe, and second, because the Dominion of Canada has had a record for integrity which is unblemished. As we have seen, the dominion government at this session has gone to considerable lengths to reinstate the credit of one of our provinces which, owing to dire circumstances, had to make an adjustment on its bonds.
The minister still does not admit that there was a breaking of the government's word. Should it be shown that there was a breaking of the government's word, as I have endeavoured to indicate on several occasions by presenting the facts of the case; if the government 5 free to break its word in regard to contracts of its own making, it is quite free to break contracts in connection with government bonds and arbitrarily lower the rate of interest or otherwise do what it will. If that should come about, or the impression should gain ground that the dominion government is not

to be relied upon, the credit of our country would suffer, and the cost to the country of its financing in the future would be very great.
To bring this matter to a head I would ask the Minister of Finance three simple questions which I think go to the heart of the matter. If he answers them as I think the facts indicate they should be answered, I will rest the case there for the present. Will the minister, having regard to the evidence which I have brought before the committee, admit that in the result these government annuities were bought through misrepresentation by the agents of the dominion government in regard to the future of government taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer is no.

The minister will not admit that, notwithstanding the fact that the government booklet has it in printed evidence, that the annuities branch of the Department of Labour admits that its members went about advertising these annuities as free of tax, and that the contractual element in regard to the option is also as valid in law and as binding on the dominion government as is the nfain part of the contract itself. Was there sufficient evidence of the existence of an optional or contractual right on the part of the holders of these annuities or annuity contracts purchased prior to 1940 to make him feel that it was necessary to pass section 5 (1) (k) of the Income War Tax Act of 1940, whereby the rights of annuity holders were done away with, even though the act itself says:
. . . provided that such exemption shall not extend to that portion of the income which exceeds the amount of the annuity actually specified in the contract before the twenty-fifth day of June, 1940, where such excess amount arises by reason of any option or contractual right to enlarge the annuity income by the payment of additional sums or premiums, unless such additional sums or premiums, have actually been paid before the said date.
It is strange that parliament, exercising its sovereign power to do what it will, found it necessary to say that even though there might have been an optional or contractual right, that right no longer existed so far as this act was concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did not say that.

Why was that put in,
may I ask?

speechtext: That simply said that if the right to take up the option was exercised after the passing of that act, the option would have to be taken up in the light of the new dominion conditions. It did not deny the right to take it up.

the holders of the option or contractual right to take up their option. The third point is this: Where there are two rulings given by the Department of National Revenue in regard, not to the enlargement of the contract from a smaller amount to the maximum of $1,200 but to the amount of the contract for whatever sum is stated

perhaps six, perhaps twelve hundred dollars. After section 5(1)(k) was passed in 1940 stating that these contracts could be matured at an earlier date than that specified on the face of the contract through the annuitant using his right under the option clause which is embodied in the contract, was there a ruling to the effect that the maturing could not be subject to tax? Then was there later a ruling given that any maturing of the contract beyond the amount stated on the face of the contract would be taxable? If so, have there been two rulings? And what is the position of those who matured their contracts subsequent to June 25, 1940, up to the present time? Some people operated under the first ruling, and now a second ruling of the Department of National Revenue, I understand, has been given. Will the minister clarify that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
The answer to the hon.
gentleman's question is no. The rulings in the main have been consistent. There may have been some slight adjustment or variation, and it is possible that some official may have written a letter which was not in consonance with the ruling of the department.

What the Minister of
National Revenue has stated is not quite good enough. I asked a simple question; was there a ruling by the department that the maturing of a contract even subsequent to June 24, 1940 was not taxable, and then at some subsequent time another ruling that

a maturing of such a contract was taxable? There are two questions to which the minister may answer yes or no.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I do not think that I can enlarge on the answer which I have given the hon. gentleman. It would be utterly impossible to examine into letters which have been written by any or every employee of the department. But the answer still holds, that in the main the ruling has not been changed, but it may have been subject to some minor adjustment.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
