speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-Deductions for superannuation or pension fund.

I wish to ask the minister a question with regard to the hardship-I think it is a great hardship-wrought by these amendments, if I understand them correctly, with regard to a considerable number of pension funds which have been set up pursuant to the rights reserved in section 5, subsection 1, paragraph (h) of the act. As I understand it, the effect of this is that in a good many pension funds which have been in effect, and where payments have been made, the rights to receive a pension tax-free are now being drastically cut down. I should like the minister to tell me if I am stating the fact correctly, and whether he does not agree that in a large number of funds which have been in operation for a considerable period of time, this drastic cutting down of rights is causing serious injury to the funds. If so, is it in his opinion necessary that this be done?
Jackman.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to persons
who have been contributing to funds under the existing provisions of the law, their position, at the time when they receive their pensions, is changed by this legislation, in respect of taxation. In some cases it is improved and in some cases it is made worse. I think that the treatment, subject to something which I am about to say with reference to the whole question of apportionment on . a cash basis, is perfectly fair. But it would be idle for me to deny that it is changed.
Take the case of a pension fund which elected to receive its investment income free of tax. That is the class of cases under the subsection which the hon. gentleman mentions. The consequences flowing from that in the past have been these. The contributor, the employee, is not entitled to deduct his contributions to the fund from his income for taxation purposes, but when the time comes for him to receive his pension he gets his pension free of income tax. That is being changed. In the future it will not be possible to set up funds like that at all. The income of the fund will be free of tax, but the pensioner, the contributor, in every case will be entitled to deduct his contributions from his income for tax purposes and he will be taxed in full on his pension. That will be the case with regard to pension funds which are set up in the future. With regard to the past there is apportionment, and the question is, on what basis the apportionment should be made. Now, the basis laid down in the act is this. We take the proportion of the total contributions to the fund which were paid in during the period when the contributions were not deductible by the employee, and the proportion which those payments in bear to the total payments in is the proportion which will be applied to the pension for tax purposes. So when the pension comes out, that proportion is applied and part of the pension is free from tax and part is taxable.
Various alternative plans have been suggested. One was to make the apportionment on a time basis rather than on a cash basis. That has much against it. Another plan was to give some weight to interest payments, which would involve actuarial calculations, and that would be the fairest basis. I have prepared a statement to deliver to the committee on these problems, and perhaps I should read it.
The purpose of paragraph (h) under subsection 1 of the section, on page 4 of the bill, is to define "a portion", or more strictly "a proportion" of a pension which shall be tax-free in the hands of the recipient employee

Income War Tax
or his dependents, because the employee, in making contributions to the pension scheme, has not been permitted to'deduct some or all of his contributions from his income for tax purposes. Such deduction of contributions from income could not be made in the case of pension funds where the trustee or corporation in charge of such funds has elected in the past to have the income from the investment of the funds exempt from taxation. In other words, under paragraph (h) of the act as it has been up to date, there have been some pension funds where the contributor was taxed on the contribution when it went in, and in return was allowed to receive a portion of his pension free from tax.
We are now changing the law in accordance with the recommendations of the royal commission to make all contributions to the pension plan deductible from income for tax purposes and to provide in general that pension payments shall be subject to tax. In order to be equitable, however, it is necessary to make an allowance for pensions which the employees have earned through contributions which could not be deducted from income, and to allow them a corresponding proportion of the pension free from taxation. This paragraph in the bill is intended to do that. The proportion of the pension which is to be free of tax is defined as equal to the proportion which the aggregate of the amounts of the contributions paid by the employee, which he was not entitled to deduct from his income, forms of the total contributions paid by the employee.
This basing of the proportion on the amounts paid under the one system and the other is the same principle which has been in the law for some time in paragraph (h) of subsection 1 of section 5 of the act. It has been necessary for some time to have a principle of this kind to cover cases where the status of contributions is changed by reason of the pension plan coming under the section after some period on the other basis.
My attention has been called to the fact that the principle on which this apportionment has been made and will be made under the law as we propose to amend it, while relatively favourable to older employees, who will be retiring shortly, is relatively unfavourable to younger employees who will have some period under the new system before retiring. The reason for this is that the formula we have been using, and which we propose for the time being to continue to use, includes accumulation of interest on contributions made to the fund and therefore weights all contributions equally in determining the tax-free portion of the pensions; whereas, strictly speaking, the earlier contributions are of more
importance in earning the pension rights for the employee, because they accumulate an interest over a considerable period.
It has been suggested that we should offer an alternative formula which would take this factor into account. Such a formula, however, involves the introduction of certain actuarial principles and in its administration would require some actuarial investigations in connection with funds and payments out of them.
I have not been prepared to introduce this alternative system at this stage, but I am prepared to consider an alternative of this kind in the future. I understand that the present proposal would not work unfairly in the immediate future and therefore there will be an opportunity for further consideration of the appropriate1 formula and preparation for its administration.
I am told I said that the actuarial-calculation method would be the fairest. I do not think I should admit that. It is alleged by some that it would be fairer than the application of the straight apportionment on a cash contribution basis. Certainly it would be preferred by many to the present arrangement. I do not know whether the point the hon. gentleman has in mind is the one I have covered.
There are pensions in connection with which employers have made by far the largest part of the contribution to the fund and where employees have been contributing perhaps for only a year or two. If the trustees of the fund made the election provided for in the law as it is at present, those employees would be entitled to receive their entire pension tax free, provided their contributions were all made after that election.
Mr. MACDON'NELL (Muekokia-Ontario): And they pay the taxes.
Mr. IiLSLEY: They pay the taxes themselves. If we are talking on the basis of fairness, however, that arrangement is not fair to the crown, because the employer may have made a very large contribution to cover fifteen or twenty years in the past. If the employer is a taxpaper he is allowed to deduct that contribution from his income for his tax purposes and it goes into the fund without any cost to the employee, because the employee did not pay it. That is not a case of the employee making contributions over that period and nevertheless paying income tax on them. After a certain date, all he needs to do under the law as it stands at present is to make one contribution. So long as he makes one contribution he is entitled to draw his pension. If he makes one contri-
Income War Tax

bution after the date of election he is entitled to draw a pension for the rest of his life and not pay income tax on it, although he never suffered any deduction except one during his lifetime in respect of his payments in. But he gets that income free of tax on the way out.
My hon. friend will say, Well, that is what the Jaw gives him at the present time, and you must not take away from him anything that the law gives him. But if we cannot alter the expectations of pensioners in respect of those plans, we cannot do any of this. Take the case of a certain bank. I shall not mention any particular one, but the employees of the bank that I have in mind have been paying income tax on the entire amount of their incomes without the deduction. They had the expectation that they would receive their pension tax free. From now on we are going to tax at least part of their pension. That is an alteration of their expectations; it is an alteration of what might be called their rights; it is an alteration of what would be their rights if we did not change the law, but I do not think that we can ever put this on an optional basis.
They did not think that the law would be changed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We cannot put this on an optional basis for every employee in Canada. It is a change in the tax system which on the whole is fairer than the old arrangement, and is recommended by the Ives commission as a good thing to do. Take the case that I put a while ago. It is entirely indefensible from the standpoint of the treasury and the taxpayers as a whole.
That was exceptional. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What has been brought to my attention is the case where there have been about fifteen years of contribution covered by the employer and two years contribution by the employee, resulting in a hundred per cent exemption of tax of the employee in expectation. That expectation is being frustrated by this change, but the employee is being treated perfectly fairly. For the years that he did make a contribution he will get credit during the pension period, but for the years during which he did not make a contribution he will be taxed on his pension.
His contribution was in labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. If it had been represented in money he would have paid taxation

on it. The whole reason why he is tax free on his pension is that he pays taxes on his contribution.
Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario) If we are considering now what would be fair, as the minister has fairly stated many people will be deprived of what might be called their expectations, or, but he added, "what might be called their rights." That is a fair way to put it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said, what would, but for this change in the law, have been their rights.
I think the minister said, "what might be called their rights." I wrote down what the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not take down the rest of it. I said, "what would be their rights if the law had not been changed.

Actually this means a grievous change in the expectations of a substantial number of people. Instead of getting tax free the pension which represents, as the minister has so fairly pointed out, not only their own payments,but the payments of the employer, they are going to get only the exemption in respect of their own payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the employer's contribution during those years in which they make payment. It must be borne in mind that they get the benefit of that as well.

Let us face the facts. So far as these people are concerned there was a firm commitment that is now being taken away. I am not arguing that there must never be a change; I am not arguing that governments must never change their tax system because it is going to hurt people's expectations. But surely you must have regard to the existing situation. I admit that there is a certain regard being had for the proportion which is allowed here, but let us take a case similar to that which the minister mentioned. A pension has been set up for older employees. The firm makes substantial contributions to take care of the past, and the employees begin to put in their own contribution. They pay income taxes on their own contributions and look forward to the time when their pensions fall due, believing that they will be tax free. This makes a drastic change in their set-up and alters the whole picture. In order to accept this new situation, must we work this grievous change

Income War Tax
on these people? Can we not accept the situation which has existed and make a sort of easement out?
I am not referring to individual cases; what I have in mind is making such provision that those pension funds which have existed can run on and be eased out in some manner other than the one suggested here. The easement the minister is suggesting is practically no easement at all. There is a hardship. I suppose the minister will argue that when there is a change in the tax system there is always a hardship. I earnestly suggest that here there is a terrific hardship on a large number of people who are coming to the time of retirement, and their whole expectation, their whole future, will be turned upside down. Nothing less than that is happening to them, because a man who is just coming to his retirement age and who has been figuring on getting an income which is probably none too large to begin with, will find himself in a difficult position. He will have to do some close figuring anyway. His pension may be SI,800, 82,000 or $2,500. If that is taxed: at the present rate it upsets his whole expectatipn in the future. The minister has agreed that the expectation is a legitimate one. These men have been working toward it for years. Can the minister say that such, a drastic and grievous upset in the expectation cannot be avoided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly there is nothing unfair about the method of taxation that is being imposed, except to the extent that perhaps something other than a cash basis should be considered, what is called an actuarial basis; but that does not meet the point of the hon. member.
Surely the minister will agree that when this was set up it was no doubt argued1, perhaps even by him, that that arrangement was a fair one, and people have acted on it for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot do any more in this bill than I have done. There has been endless discussion about this from everybody who gets worse treatment. The ones who get better treatment as a result of this are not heard from. It is a fair way of treating them, subject to the qualifications I mentioned, that perhaps weighting should be given to the interest. Between now and1 the next budget I should be willing to give consideration to this. I cannot make any change in this bill.

Is the minister saying that he intends to give consideration to putting in the qualifications,
which will be comparatively small, or is he saying that he will give consideration to the broader point which I have raised? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Divide it on the basis of employer contributions as well as employee contributions.

I mean consideration of the fairness of bringing to an end the arrangement whereby the pensions were to be enjoyed tax free. That is what I am suggesting; in other words,
5 (1) (h).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I should be willing to give consideration to that between now and the next budget. I do not know what we can do. I would not offer much hope that we can make any change except in the one respect I have mentioned, but I am willing to give it consideration. I do not see what we can do except go the whole length of giving every employer an option.
I appreciate the difficulty. I also appreciate the minister saying that he will give it consideration.

Certain companies really do not have a tax bracket; they are merely trustees, as it were, and therefore there is no substantial exemption if they are allowed to make contributions. The minister may know certain classes of companies of that sort, financial companies and so on. If both the employer and the employee make contributions to the fund, and both pay tax on their respective contributions, when the money is drawn out by the beneficiary is it taxable or non-taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The employer never pays tax on his contribution, as far as I know.

The employee would be the ultimate beneficiary, but the whole fund is built up by contributions from both the employer and the employee on which tax has been paid. Ultimately the employee benefits. Under these resolutions would that be taxable or non-taxable? The fund is created from tax-paid moneys on the part of both contributors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Moneys which have not been claimed as a deduction for tax purposes.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It always is claimed as a deduction by the employer. It is a cost of doing business.

It is in connection with an approved plan, but I am thinking of one case in particular. Possibly it is not worth
Income War Tax

while claiming the exemption because it is such a small part of the total cost of operation. The fund is built up entirely of tax-paid contributions. When the beneficiary gets the benefit under the retirement plan is the amount taxable or non-taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman talking about plans that are not approved?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is an approved plan the employee pays on the whole thing; he pays on the whole income without the deduction, or he should. On the other hand the employer could claim it as a deduction, could he not? I should think the employer would make that deduction as a cost of doing business.
Suppose he does not care whether or not he gets it. I am only interested in the beneficiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then the question is what happens to the pension when it is paid. It is fully taxable, is it not?

Suppose he has gone through the formality of obtaining approval from the minister, but without any request for tax deduction on the part of the employer, and certainly none on the part of the employee. Would there be any freedom from taxation on the amount ultimately going to the beneficiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he obtained the approval?
Yes. I do not know what good the approval would do except to qualify it under some section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The approval has this effect, that the employee may deduct the contributions from his income for tax purposes.
But when he gets the money it is taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is taxable in any case, any money he receives, apart from these apportionment cases. You are talking about a fund that starts now, and pensions are all taxable from now on.

I should like to call the attention of the minister to something which may result in hardship to employees many years from now. A man may have paid in to a pension fund for ten years; he may not get his pension for another thirty years. Unless there is something in the rules and regulations which will enable him to get a statement up to date, he will not know how much was paid in before this new act came into force. It is the employee who will have to deal with the department, and unless he [Mr. Jackman.}
knows what he has paid in up to now he will never be able to make a statement. In the past it has not been important to keep track of what he has paid, but some regulation should be passed now providing that employers will have to give statements as to the contributions to date of the different employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely he could get a statement from the trustees of the fund. The fund has to know how much he has paid in order to know how much to pay him in the way of pension. I do not think there would be any trouble about getting that information.

Assume that an employee has contributed to a regular employees' pension fund for a period of years and then leaves the employment under which he was eligible to contribute that superannuation money; but the terms of the agreement between employer and employee were such that he could continue to pay into that fund. Up to the present his payments have been tax free. Would they continue to be tax free up to the amount of $900?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; unless there is something peculiar about the case that I do not understand, that normally would be so. The whole scheme of this new legislation is that the contributions are tax free.
But he is no longer in that employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not like to be too final about that if he does not continue to be an employee. I shall have to give' the hon. gentleman an answer later.
He is still eligible to obtain superannuation under that plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be a matter of agreement between the employer and the fund.

Under section 14 of the bill the increase in the deduction to $900 becomes effective only with the 1946 income and has no relation to the 1945 income. I am thinking of some large pension schemes under which the employee has the right to make greater payments than stipulated, for the purpose of increasing the pension he may receive on retirement. That is a valuable right for older employees who may be not far from the retirement age, especially in connection with pension funds which have been in existence for only a short time. I am thinking of one very good example, the civic pension fund of the city of Toronto. About 2,500 employees are affected by this particular proposal. The principle being sound of increasing the deduc-

Income War Tax
tion to $900 per annum, would not the minister consider making this provision effective with say the last quarter of 1945, instead of delaying its effectiveness until the 1946 income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would mean an apportionment of the year, that an employee could pay in up to S300 a year for the first nine months and $900 for the last three months. I think we are doing pretty well by bringing that in as of January 1, 1946. We are making a big extension of the right of deduction from income here. There are large numbers of these pensioners all over Canada, and it would be a most difficult administrative task to make all these apportionments. I do not think I should like to make a change during the year.
Could not some formula be worked out for the apportionment without making the calculation too complicated? This affects many employees who are rapidly approaching the age of retirement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we had better change that.

Then I should like to
direct a question to the minister in regard to the unusual medical expenses section, in connection with which I should like to bring two matters to his attention. The first has to do with the deduction from salary or wages referred to at line 40 on page 4, where it says:
-including the salary or wages paid to one fulltime attendant upon the taxpayer, his spouse or any such dependent, who was throughout the whole of the taxation period necessarily confined-
In other words, in respect of a person confined by reason of illness to a wheel chair or bed, the right to deduct wages or salary paid to a full-time attendant applies only where the person is ill throughout the entire taxation period. I take it that that means the calendar year. As for the person who is totally blind, at any time in the taxation period there is permission in the section to deduct the salary or wages paid to one full-time attendant upon the taxpayer. If the principle is sound that the person incapacitated by total blindness at any time during the taxation year shall be entitled to deduct salary or wages of a fulltime attendant, why should not the principle be applied also to the person who for reasons other than blindness is incapacitated? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, the principle is sound that expense incurred in respect of the wages or salary of a full-time attendant made necessary by any form of physical or mental incapacitation ought to be included within the scope of the medical expenses to be calculated under this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At a later time I shall give consideration to the hon. member's suggestion, but I should not like to make an amendment to this bill. Many blind people have incomes, and need attendants with them pretty steadily. On the other hand, if we allowed persons to add to their medical expenses the costs, salaries or wages paid to full-time attendants for, let us say, a month, during an illness, I believe the section would be impossible of administration. Checking would be very difficult. There would be a great opportunity to have an attendant who might be considered unnecessary. On the other hand, if the person is bedridden, or is confined to a wheel chair for a full year, there is not the same opportunity. This was intended to cover cripples, or other persons who might be permanently incapacitated.

If it is a sound principle to allow a deduction in respect of the wages or salary of a full-time attendant who attends a person incapacitated throughout the year, I suggest the principle should apply equally to incapacitation for part of the year. As to the matter of proof, let me point out there are many other expenses permissible under the section, and its predecessor, which are just as capable of being misused as this one might be, or as a section such as I have suggested might be. I believe methods could be found to establish proof, which would satisfy the administrative requirements of the department. I respectfully urge upon the minister that he give consideration to that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member take it that it would apply to the same attendants for the whole year?

No; it is a matter of incapacitation throughout the whole year. At present the patient must be incapacitated throughout the entire year before the salary or wages of a full-time attendant can be deducted'. If that principle be sound, then it ought to apply to incapacitation for part of the year, because the whole purpose of the section would seem to be that of cushioning the burden of unusual medical expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct.

It is certainly unusual in respect of persons completely incapacitated for part of the year. That is more unusual than it would be in connection with a preson permanently incapacitated-let us say a paralytic. The principle is recognized as being sound and I suggest it ought not to be confined to the one group. It is recognized in respect of persons incapacitated throughout the whole
Income War Tax

year and in respect of those who are blind, whether for part of a year or for a whole year. Should it not apply to those who are completely incapacitated1 in ways other than by blindness for part of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nursing expenses are allowed.

Yes; but we know that often full-time attendants are required' by families who cannot afford to pay for nurses. Under present rates of pay for nurses it is often necessary to retain the services of a full-time attendant who will work for a rate lower than that paid a nurse.
Let us consider the extreme case of a person who, by reason of an accident, is incapacitated for eleven months of the year, and for that time requires the full-time services of an attendant. Under this section the payment of wages to that full-time attendant would be disallowed. But if the person is incapacitated for twelve months he is allowed the full amount for those twelve months. Putting it in the mildest form, certainly that is an anomalous situation. The principle having been recognized:, it ought to be made applicable to incapacitation for shorter periods, subject to proper proof to the need for a full-time attendant. I believe my suggestion is eminently fair, and I would ask the minister to consider it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall take note of what the hon. member has said. This section was drawn carefully some years ago. The provision was introduced by myself, and in the beginning we limited the allowances to payments made to registered nurses. We then decided that perhaps that was too narrow an interpretation, and that it should be extended to practical nurses. The question at once arose as to who might be a practical nurse. There are many degrees of nursing. For instance, one might find a domestic servant who could do something in addition to what would be considered pure domestic service, and might to some extent look after a patient. There was so little opportunity to check that that we finally decided the test would be that of having a full-time attendant throughout the entire taxation period, and that that wrould be a fairly good indication the person in attendance was needed for some thing equivalent to nursing services.
I believe the provision with respect to blind persons speaks for itself. There can be no doubt that a blind person needs the services of an attendant, and it does not make any difference whether such attendance is for a short or for a long period of time. I cannot remember exactly the considerations

which were in our minds at the time, but I do know that the matter was carefully considered. I should not like to make any amendment at this time.
What happens is that hon. members will make suggestions when these matters are being considered, and then when we are preparing the next budget we have them in mind. We will remember what has been so strongly urged by the hon. member for Eglinton, and, after talking it over, we will decide whether or not a change should be made. However I would not care to do so at this time unless the matter were extremely urgent-and I- do not think it is. I shall give it consideration before the next budget is brought down.

I should like to thank the minister. I would draw to his attention another point which arises from the last two lines at the bottom of page 4 of the bill. This permits the inclusion of an amount expended on an artificial limb, a spinal brace, a brace for a limb or an aid to hearing for the taxpayer, his spouse or any such dependent. I draw attention specially to the words "artificial limb, a spinal brace, a brace for a limb, or an aid to hearing", and I would refer briefly to aids to seeing. Under rulings given by the Department of National Revenue, persons purchasing spectacles are allowed to deduct that portion of the amount which they pay to the optometrist which represents his professional services, but nothing is allowed on the glasses which may be prescribed as necessary as a result of his examination. I fail to see why there should be any distinction made in principle between aids to seeing and aids to hearing. If you permit the deduction of the expenditure made by a taxpayer on a hearing aid, why in principle do you deny him the right to deduct what he has paid on an aid to vision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For two reasons-much more unusual and much more expensive.

Those may be matters that affect administration. But you have this anomalous situation. A man goes to an optometrist for an examination, who prescribes the kind of lens required to correct some defect in vision. The prescription is filled by an optician. The department permits the deduction of that portion of the taxpayer's expenditure which represents the optometrist's fee for his examination, but no deduction is allowed on the cost of the lenses, which would certainly correspond to the purchase of medicine in the case of a person requiring medicine, or an artificial limb or splint.
I do not happen to wear glasses myself, but I see that the minister does, and he has had

Income War Tax
more personal experience. I know however from experience that the prices paid for some lenses are very high indeed, and their purchase bears heavily on families who may have inherited some eye weakness necessitating spectacles for perhaps three or four or five children in the family. No deduction is allowed, and my humble submission is that it is not fair to make this distinction which discriminates against those who require to purchase these aids to vision. Will the minister give consideration to that point? I would not raise it if I did not consider it important and a hardship to many people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So many people wear glasses that it is hardly an unusual medical expense at all. Glasses are one of those things that nearly all of us have to buy. Income War Tax
What is the position with regard to earned surplus before 1917?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As we propose it, the earned surplus before 1917 comes out free of tax on a winding up.
Under the present law, does it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the interpretation of the present law. That is the way it has always been interpreted. Capital surplus of course comes out free on a winding up. Earned income, the surplus accumulated prior to 1917, if it comes out in the form of dividends, is taxable and remains taxable; and the surplus between 1917 and 1939 can come out, under the provisions of the Ives report, at these limited rates of taxation.
What type of surplus will come out free on winding up? All surpluses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: AH capital surplus comes out free on winding up, no matter when it was accumulated.
Earned surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Earned surplus prior to 1917 comes out free on winding up. All surplus up to date, both capital and income, has been taxable if taken out in the form of dividends. That is, the administration have not gone behind the dividend, to see where it came from; they have just taxed the dividend. Now it is proposed to change that in respect of the period from 1917 to 1939, and that is all it is proposed to do at this stage.

It is fair that the surplus prior to 1917, when there were no taxes on income, should come out free on winding up; when the principal proprietor dies we do not want to wind up t'he company and create unemployment. The whole purpose of this new provision is to make it possible for the chief proprietor to pay his succession duties, or the estate to pay them for him. It may be that the company was largely built up prior to 1917; it may be that new developments in the industry which other competitors did not have had resulted in not very large accumulations since that time. Would it make any difference to the minister if permission at least were given to include the pre-1917 surplus under the provision of the section we are now discussing? If there is any equity attaching to the equitable distribution of post-1917 surpluses, surely it applies a fortiori to pre-1917 surpluses. Could the option not be given to the corporation to distribute pre-1917 on the same basis as post-1917?

Mr. ILSLEY': That is the argument which the hon. gentleman advanced the other night when the resolution was up: and it is hard to 'answer, there is no doubt about that. But we are meeting a situation, and I do not want to open the door too wide or go too far. This whole problem arose from the fact that, not from the pre-1917 surplus at all, everybody I think was quite willing to wind up and start with a new company or something of the kind if he could get his surplus out tax free. They can always get their pre-1917 out tax free. What they were worrying about was their surpluses after 1917. The surpluses after 1939 are going to present another problem, which is not dealt with in this bill at all. But we are just dealing with one period here, from 1917 to 1939. For the great majority of companies, at any rate, this I think solves their problems.

I am trying to collect a little revenue for the minister in this case. If they wind a company up free, the minister goes on record to this effect; he gives them the option, if they agree to do it, to include the pre-1917 surplus. Under the provisions of this act they are going to pay some tax, some extra money to the crown. Has the minister any objection if the opposition tries to swell his revenues and give that option to people? How can any harm come from it?
The minister thinks that maybe the hon. member is trying to sell him a pup.

I had two questions to ask the minister. They deal with the new section 96 of the Income War Tax Act. Provision is made in subsection 3 of that section for the manner in which the tax is to be paid: (a) provides that the tax shall be paid on or before December 31, 1946 although the right of election to take advantage of the amendment does not expire until the end of 1947, and (b) provides a second way of paying, namely, by four equal annual instalments, commencing December 31, 1947, together with interest at the rate of four per cent per annum on each instalment from the 31st day of December, 1946 to the date of payment. What is the objection to allowing a company that has not paid by December 31, 1946, to come under the alternative plan and prepay? Suppose in 1948 they are in a position to pay everything? Why should they not be allov'ed to prepay with interest up to the date of prepayment? The way the provision reads, they are absolutely bound to pay in four equal annual instalments, with interest, and I do not see that there is any harm done by giving them the right to prepay with interest up to the date of prepayment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be that is the meaning of the section as drawn, that they cannot prepay. But I am informed by the officials that the standard practice in situations of this kind is to accept prepayment with interest up to the date when they are paid, and that is what they will do in this case.

I think that this could be read by an officer of the department, having to meet the situation, in such a way that he could at least demand payment of interest up to the end of the fourth year. I suggest it would be wise to make it clear that there is a right of prepayment. It states that a private company that has elected to pay the tax under this section either "shall"' pay the tax
up to December 31, 1946 or "shall" pay in four equal annual instalments. If words were inserted there giving them the right to prepay it would do away with any uncertainty.

There has been an arbitrary deduction in the corporate accounting from earned surplus but not through the income accounting. Corporate books are not necessarily kept from the income tax people's point of view of earnings or lack of earnings. You do what you like with your own books, but when it comes to income tax there are certain rules which are laid down and which you have to follow in paying your taxes. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let. me read over 96 (1):

I understand the way

This whole question in connection with the relationship between the deduction for children and family allowances is most complicated. As a matter of fact, the whole income tax system at the present time is too complicated, and it is hoped that after the dominion-provincial conference has reached an agreement the system will be simplified.
In connection with the matter of deductions for children, may I draw the attention of the committee to the fact that under the present system of deductions from the tax rather than from income the taxpayer with a family is placed in an unfair position. For every married man with children and every married man without children the net non-taxable or non-compressible income is $1,200. This, of course, is true, except for the normal tax.
I submit with respect that the rate of taxation should be imposed only over and above the minimum necessary to each one, according to his family responsibilities or, if we put it in this way, according to the number of dependents for whom he has a right to claim deduction. It is a false principle to set the same non-compressible and non-taxable income of $1,200 for all married men, and then to impose equal rates for what is earned over and above that $1,200, with only an arbitrary deduction of $108 for each dependent.
What is strictly necessary to rear a child should not be taxable. If it is taxable the father of a family must then accept a lower standard of living. After a little calculation, we arrive at the conclusion that the more children a man has, the higher his rate of income tax with respect to the strict necessities of life. For fathers with children in colleges or universities the situation is unbearable. I, for one, would not be here to-day if the present system of deductions had existed before the war. I would not be here, nor would I be a lawyer, because I could not have gone to university. My father received only an average salary, on which he educated five
Income War Tax

sons, and it was only after great sacrifice that on his income he was able to give the five of us college and university degrees. But to-day that would be completely impossible.
Has any thought been given to the possibility of going back to the system of deductions from income instead of deductions from the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, a great deal of thought has been given to it, and may I say that I agree that that system is more desirable than the present one-with certain modifications. Before bringing down the budget this year, we worked out a new tax structure, and considered carefully the question whether that new structure should be introduced at this session. However, for the reasons I stated when the budget was presented, we thought we should introduce an interim budget having straight percentage deductions.
I think that when a new tax system is introduced that principle, fundamentally, will be adopted, although there will be modifications to take into account the necessary interrelationship between allowances to children and family allowances. However, I know at the present time'-and of course I cannot make it public just now-the lines along which I intend to proceed. There will be much difference of opinion as to whether that is the proper one. However, we have had continual trouble with this system of tax credits for children because, time after time, hon. members have argued that the tax credit per child was not sufficient for its support. The answer is that it was never intended to be sufficient to support a child.
The principle enunciated just now by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet is much nearer the proper principle; that is, that the deduction from income which is fixed should be sufficient to support the child. Before this section is carried there are a few remarks I should like to make about the whole subject of housing. In this country we have not taken advantage of the whole situation in regard to the construction of homes. Other countries have done much better than we have in the field of housing. I refer particularly to New Zealand, where in 1939 I saw houses built by the government. To me it was a most shameful thing that we would allow our lumber to stand in piles in the mills of British Columbia; while the termites were eating our lumber there, we had people unemployed; we had slums; we had stagnation and social decay. Yet in New Zealand they were able to build new homes by the thousand with our timber, and they did so because they really attacked the problem of housing in the manner in which it deserves to be attacked. I sat in the office of the minister of housing, who at that time was Mr. Armstrong, and he told me he was the happiest man in the cabinet because he had more money than he could spend. They had set up a separate department, and the appropriation was so generous that they were able to absorb all the labour available for the building of homes in New Zealand.
At the time I visited there early in 1939 they had just brought over 200 workmen from Australia, because they had exhausted all the

National Housing
available labour supply for building homes in New Zealand. They had brought these 200 carpenters in to assist in the housing project.
I had forgotten a few of the details because it is five or six years since I was there; but consulting with the high commissioner to-day,
I found that their money was provided at one and a half per cent. They were given an appropriation from their central bank and their housing corporation undertook the construction of houses. These were not considered to be temporary structures but good for sixty years. Only the best materials were Used.
The corporation buys a piece of land and undertakes housing development, and on the basis of town planning these houses are laid out in blocks. There are no two alike in a block. They avoid monotony in design and material, and the houses are planned in relation to the whole development. They consider that they can afford to charge low rentals, because over a period of sixty years these houses will have paid for themselves and replaced the money invested in them.
The houses were a joy to behold from the outside, and on the inside they were very well planned. I found, in discussing the project with the minister, that they had invited all the architects of New Zealand to submit plans and had chosen a number of designs in units of one, two or three bedrooms. At that time they did not undertake anything larger than three-bedroom units, but since then they have undertaken the construction of apartment blocks for single business people and for .married couples without children as well as for old age and blind pensioners. They are putting up these apartments for the convenience of people who need limited housing. But they are also, in their larger houses, continuing to build the larger units with the idea of giving a priority to families with children.
There are two fields here where there is a great need. It is criminal that we should penalize the mother with children. It is a dreadful thing that the mother, who is making the biggest contribution of all to her country, should find it so difficult to get a roof under which to shelter her children. Yet one has only to try to find living accommodation to discover to what an extent children are feared and abhorred and what a penalty we put upon the mother with children.
Last year in the city of Regina I started to look for living accommodation. My family had a high school girl, a child already in grade ten. I found that even children in high school are considered a menace if you are looking
for a place in which to live. I do not know what would have happened if I had had a child in a perambulator.
In this country we should definitely give priority to all the mothers who have young children. We should definitely build homes and subsidize rentals for widows with children and for old age pensioners. These are two features which will remain part of our economy. We have started to pay pensions and will continue to do so. We have started to pay mother's allowances to take care of widowed mothers who have children to bring up. These are two- groups who, because of their lack of income, cannot pay the rentals that will give them decent homes. These are two fields in which we should definitely subsidize rentals, so that those people who are in such an unfavourable bargaining position may have decent homes.
When I was in New Zealand people said to me, "I suppose everyone in Canada has a lovely home?" I wondered why they assumed that we all had lovely homes, and they said, "Well, this is your timber; we are building our homes with your timber." We in this country, who have so much timber, who have metals and all the things that go into the making of plumbing and fixtures, furniture, draperies and1 floor coverings, we, who can build and equip and furnish homes from our own resources, have no excuse for having so many of our people living under the wretched conditions in- which we find them.
I wish we would show the same concern for the living accommodation of others that we show when it comes to our own incomes. I wish I could hear a howl of welcome going up in this house to any suggestion, about improving the living conditions of our people comparable with the one we heard this morning over the bill for increasing our own indemnity. I wish we would be as enthusiastic about our mothers and children, about our old age pensioners and about people whose condition is so desperate, as we are in regard- to people who have some money to put into annuities. If we did that we would never be content until we had a separate department of housing and a generous appropriation that would- enable- us to embark upon the construction of homes, using the materials of which we have such a generous supply and the workmen who need- employment.

The minister said just five minutes ago that the last thing he wanted to do was to import the idea of capital gains or capital losses into our income tax system; yet here is a net deduction from the amount of earned surplus to be available for distribution under the new section which will be lessened by the excess of capital losses over capital gains.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This shows the necessity of definition. Capital losses may be used to . reduce a surplus, even an income surplus.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the amount by which all capital losses exceed capital profits. The profits do not augment it, but the losses diminish it. You strike a balance between capital losses and capital profits. If the profits are greater they are not added. If the losses are greater they are subtracted.

But surely the point is, in order to do substantial justice to the owners of the company, the larger the earned surplus is-in fairness to the crown-the better for them, the more justice is done; and now, under this subparagraph (iv) earned surplus i? reduced by the amount of the capital losses. There may have been a capital loss which would wipe away all your earned surplus, and that would mean that there would be much less available for distribution under this relatively favourable section than otherwise. I think I am clear in my thinking on that. It would be unfavourable to the shareholders of the company if that were to be the case. You obviously cannot add capital gains to swell your surplus, and I do not see why you should deduct capital losses to diminish your surplus, from the point of view of taxation. On a balance sheet you might do it for appearances' sake, but that is the arbitrary act of a board of directors and has nothing to do with the taxation. I do not know why you import a capital profit or loss element into this at all. Why not leave it where it was? It may bring up the question we discussed before the dinner recess: if there were capital losses and they were taken off the earned surplus there is not that earned surplus to distribute; but I submit it is just a legal technicality. If you have cash available, or can come to the treasury and borrow it, you can pay off the full earned surplus. It is just a technical accounting figure.

But that is the thing that I questioned. The report covers the income earned between 1917 and 1939. Let us assume that between 1939 and the date of election there has been a loss of income. Let us further assume that before the time for distribution actually comes there might be a turn of affairs and the company would make earnings to recoup itself. Why is there any fairness in saying that the

Income War Tax
amount which is on hand in 1939 and which would have been distributed but for the loss intervening since 1939; if that loss is recouped, why should you cut off the company from chance of having an opportunity to distribute the amount which was on hand in 1939? It does seem to me it is pressing those two words in the report "on hand", rather hard. Looking at the fairness of the situation and what I understand to be the intent and scope of .the terms of reference of that report, it seems to me that the act steps in and undertakes to alter, by reason of something which happens after 1939, a situation which existed in 1939, and which I understood was the situation with which the Ives report was called upon to deal.
I am not assuming that parliament cannot deal differently from the Ives report if it wishes to do so, but the minister is quoting the Ives report, and 1 think he is pressing much too hard on those words "on hand".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that we can get very much farther by arguing the matter. I do not think it was anybody's intention to take the earnings that the company elects to distribute and allow those earnings to be paid out under this schedule of rates. That is what is being argued for here. Why stop at the date of paying out? Why not go away into the future? It was not the intention to take income that would be earned in 1946, 1947 and 1948 and allow it to be paid out under this favourable schedule of rates.
Nor was it the intention to take what was earned in 1939 and to worsen the situation which existed in 1939,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We cannot run away into the future. We take the situation at the time they elect. They can elect on their 1939 surplus and they can distribute it.

I cannot help feeling that the drafters of this section were frightfully legalistic and not very practical. Undistributed income on hand does not mean that there is so much money or so many liquid resources in the company representing that amount. It may be that the company has assets in the form of cash, in which case its capital and all the surplus balance is an amount of cash. It may be that a company has no cash, that it has only bricks and mortar, and all the capital and all the surplus and capital surplus, or anything else must offset only bricks or mortar. But that does not say that the company cannot get working capital or cannot
have earned surplus which is distributable. The words "on hand" used in the Ives report is a loose expression if one gets down to legal terminology. What is your earned surplus on hand at the end of the year? It is simply the amount showing in your balance sheet. Take the earned surplus of a company and the liabilities; there is no identity on the asset side representing the exact amount in the earned surplus on the liability side. It is just on the one side, on the asset side, and as long as the two sides of the sheet balance under the double entry system, it is all right.
I see no significance in the words "on hand. What is likely to happen if a company finds that it had an earned surplus in 1939 which was greater than its earned surplus at the time it elects to operate under this section of the new act? Either the company have been doing so poorly that they have had losses, or they have been doing rather poorly but have paid out more in dividends. If they have paid out more in dividends I think the minister will be satisfied that the government will get ^ its share; that is, if they paid out more in dividends than they earned' and thereby reduced the earned surplus. There should be no hesitation on his part to allow the company to take its 1939 earned surplus as the basis for distribution. I do not see that there can be any very favourable position for a company that has reduced its earned surplus, that has had either a loss or has paid out more money than it has earned. The government gets a higher rate of taxation on it, and it could not be prejudicially affected by that action under this section whereby the 1939 earned surplus is reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should just like to hear what my hon. friend would say if the Department of National Revenue exercised its powers under the Income War Tax Act to compel the payment of surplus out in dividends and then refused to permit a deduction of capital loss. I know my hon. friend would say that there was no surplus then, to the extent of the capital loss.

What about the other
suggestion?

speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver South, whom I always wish to accommodate, made a suggestion.

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES
speechtext: In the report on reconstruction, dealing with housing and community planning, at pages 110 and 111 we have some interesting paragraphs regarding tenant families in the lower third of the income bracket. It points out that in the twelve metropolitan areas the average family earnings would be $703 a year. On that basis, accepting the definition the minister has given, people living in those areas should pay rent of about $12 a month. In some of these cities the average is a great deal less than $703. In Saint John, New Brunswick, for example, the average annual family earning is $595. In Windsor it is a good deal higher, $943. I understand that about 177,000 families in Canada fall within this range, with an average of $703, and as I have pointed out on previous occasions it is very difficult for people in that income group to find places to live. Those who are being discharged from the services are finding it almost impossible to secure living quarters right across the country, and I think at this session the minister should give some indication as to what the administration has in mind to make housing available for people getting less than $1,000. I do not think the legislation now on the statute books will make it possible for life insurance companies or any builders to provide suitable units that can be rented at $12 a month. I believe some authority, either municipal, provincial or federal, must be prepared to bridge the gap between what these families can afford to pay and what might be regarded as an economic rent; and in my opinion the federal government should take that responsibility. We are all very proud of the performance of the minister during the last several years, when a difficult job had to be undertaken. ' We were told that if it is physically possible somehow or another it will be made financially posible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

National Homing
Again in this report we have a section on Philadelphia. At page 202 we are told that in the low-rental projects in that city a family getting S525 a year rents a one-bedroom apartment at $11.25 a month. A family getting from $526 to $700 will pay $14 for the same accommodation. A family getting from $700 to $900 will pay $17.50, and a family receiving from $900 to $1,200 will pay $22. Hon. members might assume there would be some friction when people living in the same apartment block find that one family is paying twice as much as another, but a good socialist principle has been accepted, that they should give according to their ability, and those who are getting twice the income of the others do not complain because they have to pay twice the rent for exactly the same quarters. If you have a larger family and require four bedrooms, and are getting less than $525 a year, you pay $12.75 for a modern apartment. If in the United States in the ten years before the war they were able to appropriate funds to build houses for their people in these low income brackets, it does seem to me that in the closing hours of 1945 we in Canada at least should be prepared to pass legislation that will provide a bridge between what people in the lower income brackets can pay and what must be paid, so that housing may be made available to this very large group in the dominion.

INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

Before we pass section 8 I should like to draw once again to the attention of the minister his statement of August 5, 1944, as reported in Hansard, to the effect that the government does not believe that a building programme invoking the assistance of municipal or provincial bodies is necessary, and that this legislation is framed accordingly.
When discussing section 5 before recess the minister indicated that in all probability housing accommodation would be made available to other than those in low income groups. I foresee a situation in which all the housing we will provide under this measure will be made available to people of moderate rather than of low incomes.
The minister has definitely stated that housing corporations sponsored by provincial governments or municipalities are not to be considered in any way under this measure. My home city of Regina has been forced

National Housing

during the fall and winter to build about a hundred temporary shelters to look after part of the requirements of our citizens. These are certainly no more than shelters, because most of the amenities of living do not exist there. At a cost of something over 1100,000 only a roof is supplied, and in two years that money will be wasted. That, it is considered, is the approximate life of the buildings being erected. Certainly these cannot be called homes.
Under present financial arrangements it is possible that the minister will secure a maximum of about 100,000 homes. This number of homes at $4,000 would amount to $400 million, which is to be made available through the use of five per cent of the assets of the insurance companies, plus guarantees by the dominion government. That would provide 100,000 homes or, according to the Curtis report, about one-seventh of our present shortage. In any event, our municipalities or private owners must supplement what the minister is prepared to do, by the terms of the various housing acts. He has said that free enterprise will be permitted to handle this emergency, and yet in answer to the hon. member for Mackenzie he said that it was physically impossible to build these houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES
speechtext: I had a communication just this week from the carpenters and joiners union of my city, in which they point out that they have seven carpenters unemployed. That may not seem like a large number, but those seven carpenters are unemployed because there are no materials to work with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES
speechtext: I point out to the minister that he has not taken positive steps to secure materials. In the first place, we are turning over large sums of government money to the mortgage and investment companies, and, by this measure, we are guaranteeing profits on their commitments to the extent of two and one-half per cent of their invested capital. Then we are not taking adequate steps to make sure that the materials produced in Canada remain here.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

has not heard those who represent agricultural communities complaining about the fact that we are selling under the world market. We feel in duty bound to assist world needs to that extent. But when one hears our lumber merchants talking about the price of hemlock-

Why does not the minister keep those supplies at home, so that carpenters can go to work? Why does he not give some impetus to apprenticeship, or to a training plan to have more carpenters on the job? We were told a few days ago that money was not the difficulty, and that it would not be a limitation in the building programme. Pour in the money; heaven knows we have been doing it for five years in connection with the war. We did not stint, because we had to get the materials.
We have those materials in Canada. We may need a little more coordination and, for a time, we may have to place an embargo on exports of building materials. We may have to train more builders. Those builders in the prairie provinces who are unemployed during winter months, because materials are not available, under proper planning could be working on housing.
We have the money; we can get the materials.; we can train the men. There are all sorts of men still in the services who would be glad to assist in this programme. Why in heaven's name can we not go to work on it? This is a national emergency, and still we are fiddling around, guaranteeing mortgage companies two and one-half per cent on their investments in connection with the building of houses. Then the minister tells us it is likely these will not be low-rental houses anyway, and that they will be taken by those in the middle-income group. The low-income people cannot afford to rent houses costing $4,000.

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

National Housing
The chief shortage is not that of lumber. The bottle-neck is in connection with soil pipe and brick.

to reconsider his definition of "approved lending. institutions" to make it possible for corporations like my own city to go into this business. speechtext:
There has been no suggestion that the municipality of Regina would form a 47696-2I8i
limited dividend corporation and take advantage of the loans on the very favourable terms provided by the act. Some municipalities might. I am not sure. There has been a suggestion or two which would come under that description and one is under consideration at the present time. But for the reasons which the hon. gentleman has stated we are fighting shy of these arrangements under which a junior government puts up a very small sum of money and the federal government puts up 90 per cent of the money because, as I stated at the time, business relations between the federal government and junior governments are sometimes a little difficult, and one can never tell when the difficulty is going to'crop up because there is a general feeling that the federal government is fair game; that if you can get what you want out of the federal government, you do. Another reason is that a great many municipalities are not preperly set to give independent and proper management to this business. speechtext:
The experience of continental countries is that public housing is the' only solution for the housing situation. I am speaking of capitalist countries too, not only socialist countries. Capitalist Britain had to go into a scheme of housing under public housing authorities, and they put up over one million houses from 1919 to 1939. That scheme was a success. They put up houses which rented for eight shillings a week. That was the average rental for a four to five-roomed house. In answer to the hon. member for New Westminster, who queried the hon. member for Qu'Appelle this afternoon about rentals, let me say that in New Zealand the rentals for accommodation in a four-roomed house averaged $3.60 a week and for a six-roomed house $5 a week. We have to do the thing along these lines sooner or later, and why not now? There is one other restriction which the Minister of Finance might remove if he will give this his blessing. That is, that the municipal housing corporations
National Housing

are to-day paying too high a rate of interest. I think he will have to lop that rate of interest to encourage them to go into low-rental housing.

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES
speechtext: In support of what the hon. member for Regina City has said, I might remind the minister that following the housing experiment after the last war we went into a serious depression, but we had the minister's assurance a few minutes ago that we shall not have a depression of that sort.

speechtext: We now have the National Housing Act, and having had more experience than we had after the last war I think municipal housing might turn out differently now from what it did then. subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES
speechtext: This section 10 is a clarification. Under the act the crown puts up to twenty-five per cent of the housing loan and the lending institution seventy-five per cent. In the first instance, therefore, twenty-five per cent of any loss in respect of a housing loan is assumed by the crown. In addition, this clause authorizes the government to pay losses suffered by a lending institution on its share of the loan up to fifteen per cent of the total investments by the institution. Actually the guarantees vary in accordance with the size of loans and the location of the houses, varying inversely with the size of loan and directly with the remoteness of the locality. In other words, special encouragement is given the'building of small homes located in outlying areas in which lending institutions would not ordinarily invest. The hon. gentleman says that fifteen per cent is unnecessarily high having regard to the experiences of the past. But the National Housing Act began to operate about 1935 or 1936; there has been a rising real estate market from that time to this, and it is the most favourable period in the world to take. There naturally would not be any losses when values are getting a little higher all the time. It is not necessary to draw the conclusion that we shall have a depression from the apprehension that perhaps real estate values will not continue to rise trom now on. The point I wish to make in this connection is that in efforts to assist in this respect-that is, to assist communities with their planning so far as housing is concerned, and I mean houses that are 'being built under the provisions of the act-there has been too much interference on the part of the planning bureau, within the housing administration, in the affairs of the local municipalities. I have myself seen evidence of it. These municipalities are not all badly governed. The minister indicated in his remarks a few minutes ago that some municipalities were not to be entrusted with the formation of limiting housing dividend corporations because they would not give efficient management. I urge that many municipalities are efficiently operated and are thoroughly capable of running their own affairs in matters in relation to the planning of their communities, and' so far as my observation goes, there has been on the part of the housing administration, in the course of its administration of the act, too much interference with the planning in the local municipalities and the local communities.

subtopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

Because of the emergency of the housing problem, the main emphasis must now be on building houses and nothing must be allowed to stand in the way. The hon. member thinks that perhaps we should not insist on that; that the dominion should not interfere in the matter of community planning. But one of his colleagues the other night, when the other bill was up, made a sustained plea for dominion assistance, and upon adequate community planning as a national policy as something that the dominion must insist upon. Administrative insistence on higher rather than on lower standards of planning has been all to the good. We were on this item the other day when the minister was called away from the chamber while I was on my feet, and I think what I have to say I might say now on this item. I wish to say a word or two about the use of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on certain occasions. Practically all the members of this group have gone on record at various times in maintaining that the police are too readily used by the government, in the case of the strike, for instance, at Windsor. I object strongly to the use of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at Windsor and-
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member will have to wait until we reach the vote for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
