Would the Minister of Justice say why James Franceschini, a wealthy contractor of Toronto, after being interned when Italy became our enemy was released before the end of the war?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member informed me that he was going to ask some question about the internment and release of James Franceschini. I think the information has already been made public. I wrote a letter to his solicitor on May 24, 1943, of which copious extracts were published in. the Montreal Daily Star of June 15, 1943. This letter, as I say, was addressed to the solicitor. He wrote me on May 25 thanking me for the letter, and then wrote me again on May 31, asking me if he would be free to give" reason-
able publicity to the terms of my letter. I wrote him back that I had his letter of May 31, and that "the letter I wrote you on May 24 was not intended to be a personal communication to you but a letter in the ordinary course of business correspondence addressed to you as Mr. Franceschini's solicitor." After receiving that letter of June 10, the solicitor evidently communicated a portion of the letter of May 24 to the Montreal Daily Star, which published it, and the following is an extract:
In the case of James Franceschini I have no objection to stating to you now that Mr. Justice Hyndman, after full inquiry into all the circumstances which had prompted the internment of this man and careful consideration of the case as a whole, had reported he was satisfied and convinced that he (Franceschini) was not disloyal to Canada and would not act in any manner prejudicial to the public safety or the safety of the state,' and that it would be quite safe and proper to order his release from internment.
My predecessor . . . still had this report before him for his final' decision when he was informed that Mr. James Franceschini had become seriously ill; he then came to the conclusion that, in view of this _ illness, it was necessary that he make a decision immediately and his decision was that the releasing of Mr. James Franceschini at that time would not be likely to involve any danger to tlhe state, and he therefore ordered his unconditional release.
I have myself examined the files, and I am satisfied that that was a proper conclusion to reach.
That. is the opinion I gave the solicitor for Mr. Franceschini after making a personal examination of the file, and I do not think there is anything more that I can add to it.

Would he be entitled to compensation for having been interned without any reason?	.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Certainly not. He was not interned without any reason. The reason he was interned was that this country was at war with Italy and there were regulations in force which empowered the then minister of justice, my predecessor, to order the internment of such people as he felt might be a danger to the state. He had at that time information of a confidential nature that an organization had been prepared to carry out sabotage in this country, and from the information he had he was not convinced that this man had done anything wrong but he was fearful that he might do something which would be injurious to the safety of the state; and because we were at war, and because, when we are at war, it is necessary to do some things which may be injurious to individuals for the safety of the whole community, he had him interned.

Supply-Justice
The hon. member has done what I have done bn a good many occasions; he has taken an umbrella out in the morning because it looked like rain, and he has not come to the conclusion that he was wrong because it did not rain. This man was interned because, to the then minister of justice, it looked as if he might be dangerous. After the facts were fully investigated he came to the conclusion that he would not be dangerous and ordered his unconditional release.
I do not think that under these conditions there is any reason for compensation. It is unfortunate for the individual, but a very large number have been interned. Internment is not punishment, it is merely a precaution which is taken under extraordinary conditions.

I am not rising to defend the gentleman in any way. I do know that after war broke out, in the city in which I live, many Italians were interned, and one of them was the gentleman referred to, whom I had known, I suppose, from twenty to twenty-five years. The late minister of justice of course, had his reasons for interning him. It is not for me to find fault with his judgment, whether in interning him or in releasing him; I merely rise td express my feeling that many Italians whom I have known for years in that end of the city of Toronto, merely because we were at war with Italy, were interned, although they were men who in the previous war had supported our cause, and maybe James Franceschini had in the Great War done his part in supporting the allies. I know some, living where he lived-for quite a long time he resided on Dufferin street, Toronto-who did their part in the first great war,-but who, on account of the scare when the recent war broke out and we became involved with Italy, were unjustly interned; and I have often said to myself, if it is now found out that any of them were interned unjustly the least we can do is, perhaps, to apologize to them for having done so. I am not saying for a moment that this man was interned unjustly; I do not know. I have read, of course, that many of our own people were interned in Italy. They, too, may have been interned unjustly, and if we apologize to those Italians here, perhaps our nationals should be apologized to in Italy. All I wish to point out is that many things have been done which should have not been done.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The hon. member
remembers, of course, that what happened during the first great war as to the conduct of Italians would not have any effect upon what they might be likely to do in the second great war. The first time they were on our side.

What progress, if any, is being made in the department with reference to the matter of petitions of right? It has been such a sore point for so long, and I think the courts and the bar are looking for some leadership in this matter. I know the Minister of Justice has had this matter brought actively before him for a long time. When may we look for some action in the direction of elimination of petitions of right in actions against the crown?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not while I am Minister of Justice.

Does the Minister of
Justice not contemplate any relaxation of the present requirements? Is the crown, in an era like this, when the activities of government are expanding farther and farther into almost every realm of business and industry, going just to hide under the protection which it enjoys at the present time?
Mr. gT. LAURENT:	No, the crown does
not hide under the protection it enjoys at the present time. I do not know of any refusal of a petition of right in the four years that I have been in the department, and I think I have arranged to have the petitions considered with due expedition. They are granted, and when they are granted the case goes to the court. What would be involved in abandoning that position would be an acceptance of the jurisdiction of the provincial courts in claims against the crown.
This matter was seriously considered when the Exchequer Court Act was amended to make the position here better than it is, from the information I have, in the United States or in any other British dominion. We have now stated that the crown is responsible for the acts of its servants and that men in the armed forces are to be regarded as servants of the crown. I do not think you will find that paralleled in any other British dominion. The question whether or not there should be an abandonment of the Exchequer Court Act and acceptance of the jurisdiction of the provincial courts in claims against the crown was considered, and it was decided after full consideration that it would not be done, that it was desirable to have claims against the people of Canada-because the crown, after all, is nothing but the representative of the people of Canada-whether those claims arose in one province or another, decided according to some uniform system and on the same basis, and that it would not be desirable to have motor accidents, for example, dealt with
Supply-Justice

by the local courts in the several provinces and in the several jurisdictions of each province.
That was gone into fully. A decision was arrived at and I accepted it. I will not raise the question again with my colleagues.

It ought to be possible to confine jurisdiction in claims against the crown to the exchequer court without maintaining the position of the crown with respect to petition of right. It is one thing to confine jurisdiction to the exchequer court and another matter to insist that claimants against the crown first obtain permission to sue the crown.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It may be humiliating to claimants to have to' ask for permission, but they do get it and go before the court and have their cases tried. That has been going on for a very long time, and I do not see that the fact of having to resort to that form is any serious impediment in the obtaining of justice. It would be otherwise if hon. members were asserting that petitions filed were improperly dealt with, that fiats were improperly withheld, but I do not think any hon. member would suggest that that is being done.

Perhaps I am wrong in asking the minister this question but when I was home last, a young man who had been released from a prison in Ontario came to my house. He had been out for two weeks and everywhere he went he would be asked, when he made application for employment, "Were you in the army?" He had not been in the army becase he had been in gaol for two years or more; I do not know how long. I am wondering how society will take care of such a young man, and there are many like him. They had nothing. They will not be able to show a registration card because the card is taken from them when they go to gaol. Now they are out they cannot say they were in the army and they have no card. What will society do for them?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Their registration cards are returned to them when they are released from penitentiaries. I cannot say what is done in the administration of provincial gaols. If they go to a penitentiary, however, their registration card is returned upon their release. There is nothing that we can do to wash out the fact that they have been convicted and have undergone sentence. It is perhaps unfortunate that there are a good many employers who do not wish to take 
someone who has been in gaol, but we cannot pass a law to force them to do so. That would not be within the federal jurisdiction.

I heartily agree.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think that all we can do is to try to foster throughout the country the spirit that those who have had the misfortune to have done something wrong and who may have reformed should be assisted in getting back into the ordinary channels of our social life. That, I think, is a matter of education and moral viewpoint that we should all endeavour to foster, because I believe there are a great many who do fall by the wayside and who can come back. Whenever anyone does something to help such an unfortunate person to come back he is doing a service not only to that person but to society at large.

Is there not an association of chiefs of police, or some such body, that tries to provide something for these men? One day I met the chief of police of Toronto, Brigadier-General Draper, in Ottawa, and he told me that he had been to. the justice department and had been in consultation with other chiefs of police and departmental officials in an effort to place such young men. Personally I think that is a very good programme, and I have been wondering if such a programme would not come under the new set-up the minister has in his reclamation service.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I hope it wall develop from that, but I must point out to the committee that this would be something along the lines of the Borstal societies that look after those who - have had the training of Borstal institutions. It was urged the other day very forcibly that we should institute a Borstal system in Canada; but I am sure the hon. member for Weyburn, who urged that, did sb for the purpose of having the matter before the public and not because he felt it could- be done here, although he did say he deplored the fact that there was nothing in these estimates for a Borstal system. He wished to see a commission set up clothed with sufficient powers to implement all the recommendations of * the Archambault commission. That may be very desirable, but this parliament could not do it. This parliament would not have the jurisdiction to do it. The Archambault report clearly sets out that the Borstal system cannot be worked out under our penitentiary system or with the jurisdiction we at present have. Members of that comnlission well knew what was the constitutional distribution of powers under our system of provinces and . central authority,

Supply-Justice
and they recommended, at page 354 of their report, centralized control. They state that a' Canadian penal system should be centralized under the control of the government of Canada, with the federal authorities taking charge of all the prisons in Canada, the provinces retaining only a sufficient number to provide for offenders against provincial statutes, prisoners on remand and those serving short sentences.
That is a matter which I hope will be developed in the course of this present dominion-provincial conference, but it will require a constitutional amendment. The federal authority has jurisdiction only over penitentiaries, and the commission pointed out expressly on pages 199, 200 and 209, that the Borstal system could not be adopted without centralized control of our penal institutions. I quote from page 199:
Your commissioners are of the opinion that -any satisfactory adaptation of the Borstal sye-te-m is impossible in penitentiary institutions, either in its essential features or in its principles.
And on page 200 they said:
Although you-r commissioners are of the opinion that -the English Borstal system cannot successfully be introduced into the penitentiaries or reformatories of 'Canada, their inspection of institutions for the treatment of young offenders
That caused them to report that it is a very good system. They finally recommended that the necessary changes be made to make it possible to have a system along the lines of the Borstal system. The Borstal system is a system of education, and education is the responsibility of the provinces. It is one of the things which I think the provinces would be reluctant to have subjected to any federal interference. It may be possible to arrive at a line of demarcation between what would be educational and what might be done to relieve them of the responsibility and burden of taking care of offenders who are not condemned to a penitentiary sentence.
That is something that I hope will be gone into at the dominion-provincial conference, although I do not expect that anything final will be decided at once. When the Penitentiary Act was amended the other day I told the, house that I hoped to be able to find someone who could take all these recommendations and go about and interview separately the representatives of the provinces and see what could be done to bring about the kind of change which would enable some authority-I am not anxious to have it done by a centralized authority; I am not anxious to have the federal government dealing with things which perhaps can be better dealt with
locally-to handle this. It may be that something desirable can be achieved through cooperative action. It may be possible to -have the necessary things done, but I do not anticipate that at any early day when the estimates of the Department of Justice are before the committee there will be any substantial sum in them for the administration of a Borstal system. There may be some contribution to some joint action by the federal and provincial authorities along those lines.
I hope that even -before that may be achieved there will be a possibility of segregating in the penitentiaries the young offenders from the hardened criminals, but that is not sufficient. It is not so much in the penitentiaries as in the provincial gaols that these contacts take place between young offenders who have received sentences of three or six months and the hardened criminals. That is something which under our system cannot be dealt with by one authority alone; there will have to be cooperative action between the federal and provincial authorities in that regard.

I welcome what the minister has said, and this whole committee should support him in whatever he finds necessary to do to bring about the reclamation of our offenders in cooperation with the provinces. I said the other night that I had made quite an investigation into the operation of the Borstal system in the old country, and if anyone else has done the same thing I am sure he will corroborate what I say. It was started in a small place called Borstal, and' that is how it got its name. It was instituted, I believe, by Sir Samuel Hoare. I listened to him make an address in the British house, and I then went to Leeds where the school was located.
My hon. friend here spoke about Borstal schools, but as far as I can find out there was just the one at that time, although there may be more now. That was in Wakefield' prison, just outside Leeds. They sent me from there to Barlinnie prison outside Glasgow to continue my studies.
I was in that prison for a day ,so that I could survey the operations of the Borstal programme. The guards and prisoners are dressed alike; no one wears a uniform, not even the warden. They were all dressed just as I am. I went out into the prison with a guard who might have been one of the prisoners for all I knew. I went from one part of the prison to the other to study the different trades that were taught. Contrary to what my hon. friend has said, they had not only first offenders but prisoners who had
Supply-Justice

been sentenced to death, but not in the same wing. I was taken into a chapel in the prison where I heard a man who had been sentenced to death playing the most beautiful music I have ever heard played on an organ; he was playing "Nearer my God to Thee". The guard or warden, or whoever it was with me said, "That is good music, because he is going to die shortly," I think it would occur after three Sundays had passed. It appeared to me to be good reclamation when they had got him that far in so. short a time. I hope the minister will use every effort to intro* duce into our prisons a system similar to the Borstal system in England.

Can the minister say anything further with regard to the remission of- the sentences of the navy and army personnel who were convicted as a result of their activities at Halifax?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not in a position to say exactly how many are left. There were several who received relatively long sentences who will be dealt with in the Christmas releases. Those who received short sentences have already been released. Those who had no previous criminal record will have their cases considered in the Christmas releases. I could not tell the hon. member whether or not notifications have gone out, but a distribution has been made as between those who could be dealt with for Christmas and those who could not. Some who had previous criminal records and who were not armed forces personnel were involved in the disturbance, and their records make it appear that they are not deserving of any special consideration. Those regarded as deserving of special consideration have been or will be dealt with in the Christmas releases. As the hon. member knows, at Christmas and Easter the releases are much more numerous than at any other season of the year. I can repeat to the hon. member the assurance I gave previously that they are being dealt with as special cases; and I do not think there will be any who had no criminal records who will not be home for Christmas.

I wish to ask the Minister of Justice a question ahd this might be as good a time as any for it. I am glad the Minister of Transport is in his seat, because it also involves his department. It has to do with Canadian nationals serving during the war on British merchant ships registered in the United Kingdom. In this case, which I have tried to iron out with the Minister of Transport, a man lost his life when his ship was torpedoed and he left some small estate con-

sisting of back wages, personal belongings and so forth. It is necessary for the next of kin in Canada to go through a great many legal formalities in the old country, to the extent of- hiring a lawyer and so on, and I was wondering if in the legal machinery of the government, which comes within the purview of the Minister of Justice, there is not some way we in this country could settle the estates of Canadian nationals who gave their lives for us, without waiting for a year or two years and spending in legal fees practically the entire amount of the estate in the old country.
I took up the matter with the Minister of Transport, who passed it back to me. He was quite prepared to do anything he could, but evidently within his department there is no legal machinery to handle the matter. This case has. been in the slings for more than two years, and is still unsettled. It has gone through the probate court, but the next of kin still has to go to the old country and hire a lawyer in order to settle up the estate, and in doing so the legal fees will almost amount to the value- of the estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I do not think the case raised by the hon. member is any different from that of a Canadian citizen who died and left property in the United States of America.

All the difference in the
world.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speechtext: This man died on the ocean.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: That may be.
He was domiciled1 in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: He was not domiciled in Canada. He was on a British ship, registered in Britain; and in accordance with the merchant shipping act of the United Kingdom his estate must be wound up in- accordance with the law of the United Kingdom. We cannot change that. All we can do in the Department of Transport is to assist the heirs in this country in filing a claim, and that we are prepared to do.

I am not a lawyer, and I am not going to argue with the minister, who is; but I heard this matter of domicile argued pretty thoroughly in the veterans affairs committee. The case of a man- leaving an estate in the United States is not analogous at all to the question we are discussing. This man lived in Canada all his life. He shipped out through a Canadian shipping office. He went on the ship in Canada, and his ship was torpedoed -in the Atlantic ocean. The estate under discussion consists merely of the wages and personal belongings of that individual. He was domiciled in this country, according to the definition of "domicile" I heard given by the legal adviser of the Department of Veterans Affairs. He had no domicile in Britain; he lost his life in the Atlantic ocean; he was a Canadian citizen; he signed up through a Canadian shipping office and sailed from a Canadian port. So that the point at issue is that the next of kin in this country have conformed to all the Canadian laws, has gone through Canadian probate, and now finds it necessary to spend practically the amount of the estate for legal fees in the old country. He consulted a lawyer in Canada and was advised to hire another lawyer in the old country, that the solicitor in Canada could not go farther.
I think it is an obligation the Canadian government owes to the next of kin of merchant seamen who gave their lives for this country at least to accept the responsibility of dealing with the British authorities in settling these estates, without expense to the next of kin in this country. I am not blaming the Minister of Transport, who is hemmed
in by red tape. I am now asking the Minister of Justice, who presides over the administration of justice in this country, to be kind enough to confer with some of the legal fraternity who surround government departments, to see if he cannot work out some means of settling these matters with the least possible expense and anxiety to the next of kin of those who made the supreme sacrifice during this war. After all, there are only a few of these cases, but an injustice is being done.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Under ordinary circumstances the Department of Justice would have nothing whatever to do with property and civil rights. It may be that the Department of Transport, because of its control of merchant shipping, under the particular circumstances to which the hon. member refers should assume the responsibility of retaining -this English solicitor; but that is quite outside anything the Department of Justice has jurisdiction to deal with. The Department of Transport can attempt to help a merchant seaman, or the Department of External Affairs can attempt to help a Canadian citizen. The Department of Justice has absolutely nothing to do with it. If the hon. member were to ask if the Department of Justice would make some of its officials .available to conduct correspondence, such could no doubt be attempted under the special circumstances mentioned by the hon. member. But it would be doing something not at all within our jurisdiction, no more than if I, personally, as a practicing lawyer, attempted to do it as a favour to a fellow Canadian. There should not be the idea-and it does exist quite broadly -that the Minister of Justice should attempt -to deal with anything that anybody considers is unjust. Fortunately for the Minister of Justice, that is not the role which has been provided for him by the constitution or by parliament.

I believe the hon. member for Cape Breton South has brought up a matter which could be settled in a simple manner. Overseas to-day, so far as the army is concerned, there is an estates branch to which a number of lawyers are attached. 100.	Branch administration, $122,344.

Mr. Chairman, I wished to speak at some length on this item, but to comply with the wishes of the rest of the house I shall take only a few minutes. As I happen to come from a constituency that has a penitentiary and a lot of my constituents are officers in the penitentiary, I am naturally quite interested in this vote.
I would draw the minister's attention to order in council P.C. 8/1751. In the operation
of that order it has been found that the guard who had reached his old maximum salary, instead of receiving the new maximum at once, * approached it only by annual increases of $60, or $5 a month, so that he reaches the new maximum only at the end of three years, while the officer recently engaged goes in at the new maximum right away.
I would suggest to the minister that all grades of penitentiary officers be granted an increase of $240 per annum. I consider that an increase in salary is justified in order to bring the salaries of penitentiary officers more in line with salaries that are paid to officers employed by other law-enforcement agencies throughout the dominion. The recent increase in salaries granted to penitentiary officers did little to improve their financial position, because the officer who was receiving the old maximum for his position has to wait for a period of years before being eligible to receive the maximum of the new salary range, which he reaches by annual increases, in most cases, of $60 a year. In that connection I should like to quote from the report of the royal commission investigating the penal system of Canada. The commission say in their report:
It is -also imperative that the pay of officers should be raised somewhat comparable to the rates prevailing in other similar services. It is hopeless to expect to get competent penitentiary officers at salaries that are considerably less than the wages paid to street cleaners in the large cities of Canada.
I wish to speak about the housing at Stony Mountain. Stony Mountain is a congested area and the housing is in bad shape. The houses on the reserve, with the exception of two, were condemned years ago. If the staff is to be enlarged, houses will have to be provided. The housing situation should have been remedied long ago. It cannot be expected that the morale of the staff can be maintained at a high level when they are compelled to live in houses that would not be tolerated in any urban centre. To back up that statement I shall quote again from the report of the royal commission investigating the penal system. The commission have this to say at page 317:
The 'accommodation for the staff is inadequate. It is unreasonable and unnecessarily humiliating to ask the members of the staff to live under the conditions that now exist in -the officers' tenements belonging to the institution. These houses were built fifty years ago; they are without sanitary conveniences, and prisoners themselves are much more comfortably housed in their cells than the officers in the penitentiary *tenements.
Your commissioners are of the opinion that this state of affairs is destructive of the morale of the officers and that immediate steps should be taken to provide the staff and their families

Supply-Justice
with respectable .accommodation. In a large metropolitan centre the homes which are provided for the staff would, indeed, be condemned by the medical authorities.
A great many of the penitentiary officers live in Winnipeg because of lack of accommodation at the penitentiary. At Headingley provincial gaol a bus service is provided for the transportation of the officers, and I would ask that a bus service be provided for the officers at Stony Mountain. I think that is a reasonable and feasible suggestion. Because of the deplorable condition of the houses in which they have to live some provision of that kind is an immediate and urgent necessity. It is recognized that security demands that a proportion of the staff reside within call of the institution, so that it would be the wise and economic course to establish a reasonable means of transportation for the officers between the penitentiary and Winnipeg. A bus should be put on to take these men back and forth. That would help to solve the problem until proper housing accommodation is provided.
I have visited Stony Mountain penitentiary and Kingston penitentiary, and I find that at both the officers are allotted according to the number of convicts. There is something wrong with that system because a penitentiary is something like a huge liner, something like the Queen Elizabeth, and requires a full crew to operate it efficiently. But by the officers being allotted on a quota basis, so many officers to so many convicts, if one of the officers is taken sick another officer has to work that extra time, and at Stony Mountain it is some time before he gets that time repaid. I do not think any man should be asked to work for more than forty-four hours a week, and if he works overtime he should be allowed time off at some time in the future or be paid overtime, whichever you like, but I know that the government does not like to pay overtime.
At both Stony Mountain and Kingston penitentiaries the officers are compelled to take their food in the prison, food which is cooked by convicts in the cookhouse. I am sure the minister must realize that the whole prison could be put out of commission by the food being poisoned. In the report on penitentiary reform it is recommended that an officer be employed to cook for the officers in the institution. As matters are, you are playing with dynamite. Men going out to work in the fields can pick up poison and bring it in and drop it in the food. It may be that a trusty is doing the cooking and that pressure would be brought to bear on him, with the result that forty or fifty officers may be made very sick.

I also suggest to the minister that vacancies in any penitentiary should be open to staff applicants all over Canada; that is, if there should be a vacancy at Kingston or at Stony Mountain it should be advertised in every penitentiary in the dominion. This would give an opportunity to men experienced in the work to secure transfers to other locations, with advantage not only to themselves but to the system at large.
My final suggestion to the minister is that the rate of superannuation should be based on the average of the last five years of service, not the last ten years.
I had a number of other things to say, but to help things along I will reserve them for some other time.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The situation with respect to housing at Stony Mountain has been investigated', and plans and specifications have been submitted to the Department of Reconstruction for fifteen new houses there just as soon as the Department of Reconstruction will allow them to be proceeded with.
With respect to the other remarks made by the hon. member, I can assure him that these matters are under active consideration and that it is hoped that, now that the man-power situation in Canada is changing, there will be considerable improvement.
I thank the minister.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Psychiatrists are called in as and when required, and at Kingston there is a part-time psychiatrist who is regularly retained and regularly visits the institution.

Could the minister give us some information, perhaps by way of a general statement, to cover the particular points I have in mind which are of interest to those who are concerned with conditions

Supply-Justice
affecting members of the armed forces serving terms of penal servitude as a result of sentences which have been imposed on them? In particular, could the minister state how many persons in the armed forces are serving in penitentiaries, and whether any are serving in civil penal institutions overseas, in England or on the continent; and, when such persons are discharged, is any distinction made in the terms of their discharge; is there anything they can show when they go back to civil life by way of making a distinction between purely military offences and the civil offences for which other prisoners have served in penitentiaries, so that they can show that their confinement to a penitentiary was the result of their service in the armed forces as distinct from a purely civil offence?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The Minister of Justice does not in practice advise with respeet to sentences imposed by courts martial. That is not something which in the practice of the departments is dealt with by the Minister of Justice or by the Solicitor-General; it is dealt with in t-he Department of National Defence or in one other of the service departments.
On March 31, 1945, there were about 400 persons who had been convicted while in the .service and sentenced to terms in the penitentiaries. They are treated as though they had been ordinary civilians convicted by the ordinary courts of justice, and are dealt with just like any other convict convicted in the ordinary courts of justice.
As to those convicted by courts martial the situation is quite different. I am informed that there are about eighty members of the forces convicted by courts martial overseas who have been returned to Canada and who are serving in penitentiaries the terms imposed on them by these courts.

And no distinction is made when they are discharged or have completed their terms, no document given to them by which they 'can, show that their penitentiary service was the result of some military offence rather than a civil offence? What I have in mind is that certain offences which carry sentences of penal servitude may be purely military.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would assume they could easily obtain from the service departments a copy of the sentence imposed by a court martial. All we have is a commitment from the court martial, but I would imagine that it would be possible for them to get some kind of certificate from the warden that they had served the sentence imposed upon them by a court martial on such a date.

Will the minister give consideration to seeing that that will be done as a matter of course?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, I will see if it would not be possible to arrange that, with respect to those who are confined under commitments issued by courts martial, upon discharge they be given a certificate that they have served such a term as a result of the sentence imposed by that kind of court.

May I ask for some information on the details of judges' pensions and the other benefits set out in the details on pages 94 and 95? I notice that under the heading of "judges' pensions" there is the name of the judge and then the name of a woman who appears to be the judge's wife. How does that happen?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Under an amendment to the Judges' Act made by the last parliament it was provided that a judge might make an option of getting, instead of the pension provided by the act in his favour, two-thirds of it in his own name and one-third in the name of his wife. Most of the jpdges made that option, so thati it now happens that some have retired and have been given in their own name two-thirds of the pension to which they would otherwise have been entitled, the other third being granted to the wife.

Does that pension continue for the last survivor?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They are life pensions.

When a judge retires and takes on some other position in the pay of the government, does he continue to receive his pension as well as the salary of the new position?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. The Judges' Act provides that if he is in receipt of a salary from the crown the pension shall be abated by the amount of the salary or vice versa. Whichever is the larger is paid and the other is not.

Are widows of judges entitled to a gratuity as of right, or is a means test applied?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They are paid under a vote that goes back a great many years. The amount is equal to two months' salary.

That is, all widows?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: All widows of judges receive two months' salary from the date of the judge's death.

Annually?

Royal Canadian Mounted Police-
312. General administration, $264,261.

There are a number of questions I should like to ask the minister in regard to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and in doing so I know I speak for all hon. members in complimenting the force on the magnificent work done during the war under Commissioner Wood. It has been one of the most creditable records of any department in that no sabotage took place in Canada in that period. What I have in mind particularly has reference to the men who enlisted from the force after their discharge. There was quite a large number of men who, instead of signing on for a further period, decided at the expiry of their terms to join the armed forces. They are now returning from overseas, and they find they are denied an opportunity of joining the mounted police except after medical examination, and subject to not being placed in the same position in which they were at the time of enlistment. I could refer to a number of cases where men who had been in the force for a period of years and had1 attained the rank of corporal or sergeant decided that their services would be more valuable in the armed forces. They joined up and are now returning, and if they were incapacitated in any way they have no opportunity of joining the mounted police to-day. I suggest in the first place 'that there should be available to these men clerical po.sjtiohs and the like which they might be able to fill so that their service may be continued; and, second, that, when- they rejoin, the period of time they were in the armed forces be taken into account as far as pension is concerned. I consider that there would be no serious disagreement if they were permitted to have the period served in the armed forces reckoned as part of the pension period.
Another point has to do with the question of service stars. My information is that by an amendment to a rule, passed in April of this year and published in the Canada Gazette, members of the force are entitled to wear stars only when they have had continuous, unbroken service. In other words, when- they are reengaged they are entitled to no stars at all. I have before me the names and records of men who gave distinguished service in the mounted police. If they are now fit for reengagement, they are being reengaged in lower ranks and are denied continuity of pension and also their service rights. These are matters that should be given consideration.
[Mr. MacNicol.l
I believe that it would meet with general approval if the necessary changes were made .to enable the carrying into effect of the suggestions I have offered in this regard.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I thank the hon. member for the congratulations he has offered the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on the efficient work they did, which, to say the least, coincides with there having been no sabotage in Canada during the war. I think that is due to the efficient work which they performed. At the outbreak of the war there was a feeling of anxiety and unrest and an appeal was made to the members of the force to stay with the force. It was pointed out to them that their services in the force would be of exceedingly great value to the nation. As to those who wished to go overseas, an opportunity would be afforded them to go as members of the provost corps, which almost at once proceeded with the troops. There were some who preferred at the expiry of their engagement to take positions in the- armed forces where there were greater advantages in the ranks or pay or allowances they obtained. Now it is felt that they should not be treated, when they come back, on the same footing as those who heeded the appeal and stayed with the force on conditions that were less favourable to them than they could have obtained by joining the armed- forces. It is considered that these men, having exercised their right, terminated their connection with the R.C.M.P. at the expiry of their engagement and should not be on a par with those who heeded the appeal, remained with the force and served with it in Canada or in the provost corps overseas.
That is a matter which has been seriously considered, and- the decision has been made by the commissioner and- his advisers that it would not be fair to allow those who chose to take the advantages that they were able to have during that period to come back and be on absolute equality with persons who did not do so but stayed with the force.
I think that covers the various matters the hon. member has mentioned. They have been offered reengagement, but they do not get the same seniority rights as those who remained with the force. The matter of whether time spent with the armed forces should count for pension purposes with respect to those who are reengaged is under consideration. This has always been done for time served with some other branch. While the matter has not been settled finally, it is under consideration, and from what has been done in the past I think it is fair to assume that the decision will be that those years will be counted. With respect

Supply-Justice
to the other matters we consider that we must give preference to those who stayed with us;
I do not mean necessarily those who stayed in Canada, but who stayed with the R.C.M.P., either in Canada or with the provost corps that went overseas.

I was glad to hear the hon. member for Lake Centre pay a tribute to the R.C.M.P., particularly in connection with the work of the provost corps in the different military centres. They carried out a very difficult task. In recruiting for the R.C.M.P. is preference being given to men who have returned from overseas?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The commissioner informs me that he is recruiting only those who have returned from overseas.

I should like to
support the statement made by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and I must say I was surprised at the statement by the Minister of Justice. Our banks and other institutions have been severely criticized at times, but they have set a good example in the tribute they have paid to their employees who enlisted. When they come back they receive their seniority rights and all increases in pay to which they are entitled. I would think a member of the R.C.M.P. who enlisted should be entitled to the same recognition. I should like to ask about pensions paid by the R.C.M.P. A man who retires is entitled to a pension, but no provision is made for his widow or family. Has any consideration been given to that phase of the matter?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The matter of pensions to the R.C.M.P. and the military forces has been under consideration for some time by an interdepartmental committee. That committee is preparing a statute which will provide substantially the same system of pensions for the militia and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The hon. member made a comparison between the banks and the R.C.M.P. Rightly or wrongly, we consider that the war service of the R.C.M.P. in Canada or in the provost corps was of a different character to service in the banks. It was something that was as essential to the war effort, to the fighting effort of the Canadian people as was service in other branches of the armed forces. It was because the appeal was made along those lines that we feel in duty bound to give some preference now as to seniority to those who heeded the appeal over those who chose to go to another branch of the armed services.

Has consideration been
given to providing that men who have retired from the mounted police can obtain treatment in the hospitals of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I know of several of these men in Vancouver, and I believe that at the present time there is no such regulation, that they have no treatment privileges in the hospitals of the other department. I think
Supply-Justice

it would be a very fair move if some such provision could be made. In any event I would ask that the two ministers give some consideration to providing treatment of that kind.
The second question I should like to ask has to- do with the security guards. Quite a few men, getting on in years, were recruited as security guards serving under the mounted police, and I believe they rendered excellent service. Would it be possible to provide that they should get some badge or something to show that they had rendered this service to the country during the war? Perhaps the Minister of National Defence would have to come into this picture, but I believe something should be done to accord these men that recognition. It may be that something has already been done, but as far as I know they are not eligible for any badge or medal or any sort of award.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They get a certficate of service, and consideration will be given to the suggestion that they be given some form of decoration which they can wear on their tunics or coats.

It was the latter group to
which I was referring.

I wish to support the views
that have been expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South in regard to the men who served in the security branch of the R.C.M.P. I came in contact with them on the waterfront, and know what they went through. I could make this a long story, but I have placed their case before the Minister of Veterans Affairs with a view to having them enjoy the benefits enjoyed by others who endured hardships, because certainly they carried out their duties in an efficient manner during the war.

speechtext:
That is a question
which might well be considered by the committee on veterans affairs when we meet again, I hope at the end of February or early in March.

On the general matter of the mounted police, according to what I see on page 7 of the report notice is given of amendments to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act having to do with part TV. Under

that act there seems to be a fund for payment of pensions to widows of non-commissioned officers and constables, and I understand that this is a fund which has been established since 1934. The commissioned officers of the mounted police also contribute to a pension fund, but to that fund assistance is given by the government. I quote what appears on page 7 of the annual report:
The only pensions available for widows of non-commissioned officers and constables at the present time are those provided by part 4 of the Royal Canadian- Mounted Police Act, and which are purchased by them on a monthly contributory basis. The fund to which they contribute was opened in 1934, and is On- a selfsupporting basis. Contributions are compulsory for men who entered the force afteT the passing of the statute, but those men who were already in the force at that time were given an option in the matter.
In the opinion of the writer, part 4 of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act as it stands to-day was only a beginning in the direction indicated, and he sees no valid reason why the non-commissioned officers and constables of this force should not receive -assistance from the government in this matter, in -the same way aa commissioned officers in the force do, -and practically all civil servants throughout the country.
There seems to be a bit of discrimination here for which I can see no reason. If the minister will indicate that he intends to bring in an amendment to the act shortly, or intends to take up this matter, I shall be satisfied with that. If not, I should like a statement from him.	,
Mr. ST. LAURENT: This is one of the things being considered by the interdepartmental committee, which is endeavouring to arrange a pension system that will be somewhat uniform for the R.C.M.P. and the permanent army, navy and air force.

In the meantime, then, I understand that the fund as far as constables and non-commissioned officers are concerned is entirely contributory and has to be selfsupporting, while on the other hand the fund for widows of commissioned officers receives contributions from the government. In other words, widows of commissioned officers will receive special treatment as compared with widows of constables and non-commissioned officers.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That was one of the things which necessitated the establishment of this interdepartmental committee. It was considered that there were discriminatory features in these superannuation provisions which the federal government makes for its civil servants, and the interdepartmental committee was set up to endeavour to bring about some condition which would not leave anyone feeling that he was being discriminated against

Supply-Justice
as compared with the treatment accorded to others. It is to try to bring about some degree of uniformity that this interdepartmental committee has been constituted.

How long has it been functioning?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: For several months now.

It is not more than a year, then?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	No. It commenced
its work some time last summer and has been at it now for several months, investigating the situation with respect to all these various branches, trying to arrive at something which would not be discriminatory as against anyone concerned, and trying to harmonize the whole thing.

Some time ago I asked the
minister a question with respect to marriage regulations in the R.C.M.P. and was informed that prior to April of this year a man had to serve for seven years before he was permitted to marry, and that in April this was modified to five years. I wish to thank the minister for modifying that Jacobean principle of having to work for seven years for a wife; but now in view of the fine things that have been said here about what a splendid corps of men they are, and how vigorous and virile they are, is the minister justified in keeping them out of circulation for five years?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The duties which fall upon the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are such that there must be a certain proportion of the personnel unmarried. I am told that 'at present sixty-nine per cent of the members are married, and that is considered to be as high as the force can go and remain efficient and sufficiently mobile. There is the necessity of having a substantial portion of the force that can be- moved about without regard to domestic obligations, and at present that is as high a proportion as the commissioner considers he can allow it to go and still have an efficient and mobile force.

Is free discharge,
or discharge by purchase now reinstated?

During recent
months have there been a large number of applications for discharge by purchase from recruits who joined during war time? What is 47696-219
the position to-day, generally, as far as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is concerned? Does the minister intend to expand the numbers in order to meet the current crime wave, and what is the shortage that is to be filled by men coming back from overseas?

What is the establishment?

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I shall have to get that information, but the commissioner tells me that it has not been larger than average.

May I speak to a question which I have discussed before? There are large numbers of these highly trained and specially skilled men doing guard duty in dominion government buildings. When I raised the point at the last session the minister said that some consideration might be given to having the guards for dominion government buildings arranged through some service other than from among the highly skilled members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Inasmuch as the force is small, and as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has tremendous responsibilities, I am wondering whether the minister might consider that some other force could be given the job, one which, while probably not ceremonial, is perhaps routine in nature.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not remember having made that declaration, but I do remember saying that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had absorbed the dominion police force.

The old dominion police?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes, and that it was found it would be convenient to have the two forces under one administration, because it afforded1 opportunities for employing men who for one reason or another had become

Supply-Justice

unfit for more strenuous duties. I am not suggesting that many of those who are doing guard work are not fit for more strenuous duties, but it has given some elasticity to the administration of the force, and the commissioner does not feel that it would be desirable to have the administration of those doing guard duty, and others, separated.
Item agreed to.

What are the rates of pay for the various ranks in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The third-class constable, holding the lowest rank, receives 81,003.75 per annum. The secondi-class constable receives $1,095; the thirdKdass, $1,277.50. the third-class constable include the cost of living bonus?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.
